Όχι μόνο με μακροπρόθεσμο, άυλο τρόπο. Το impa…
items.descriptionOriginal: Parents and educators often walk a difficult line when it comes to getting the best out of kids. Push too hard or coach too harshly, and they might shut down. But going too easy does them just as much of a disservice. However, when done right, teaching can make a world of difference. Not just in a long-term, intangible sort of way, either. The impact of steady, consistent feedback from teachers , parents, and even peers, when delivered the right way, can be downright jaw-dropping. Famous teaching case study begins with drawing of a butterfly Educator Ron Berger was a longtime public school teacher before becoming the Director of EL Education, a K-12 nonprofit that advocates for school and curriculum reform. Over his 25 years as an educator, there’s one lesson he carries with him that he continues to share with nearly everyone he meets. The story is about Austin, a former student of Berger’s. Austin, a 1st grader at the time, was asked to draw a Western Tiger Swallowtail butterfly. The Western tiger swallowtail butterfly. Photo credit: Wikimedia Commons His first attempt looked like any child’s drawing of a butterfly you’ve ever seen: big, round wings, beady little eyes, and no specific design or features to indicate the butterfly’s species. But instead of giving Austin a gold star for effort and a pat on the back, Berger kept pushing his student. Or, more specifically, he asked Austin’s peers to push him. Austin’s peers were asked for help through kind, specific feedback Berger asked Austin’s peers to help him improve his drawing through suggestions and feedback. However, the feedback instructions must be extremely intentional. When Austin’s classmates critiqued his drawing, they were asked to comment only on the drawing (never on Austin himself), be as detailed as possible in their critique, and offer specific ways Austin could improve his work. Oh, and the feedback absolutely had to be kind . Some of the initial feedback was spot on: the butterfly’s wings should be more pointy and less round. They also advised Austin to add more details true to the butterfly’s anatomy, like swallowtails or extensions at the bottom of each wing. After hearing from his peers, Austin took another shot at drawing the butterfly. Then the process was repeated with even more feedback, followed by another draft. All in all, Austin completed six drafts of his butterfly over several days. When Berger reveals Austin’s sixth and final draft to his audiences of students and teachers alike, the result is often audible gasps of “disbelief and delight,” per EL Education . See the entire journey in this video from Berger and EL Education: Simple drawings, but a treasure trove of lessons “Austin’s Butterfly” is an amazing lesson and case study that has withstood the test of time simply because it has so much to offer. Kids, teachers, and parents alike can all learn from the result. Students can see themselves in Austin and what he accomplished with a little help and a lot of persistence. The case study teaches resilience and a growth mindset that can set kids up for success in almost any arena. Berger’s lesson is also an amazing blueprint for giving feedback. Educators and parents today are careful not to crush a kid’s spirit with tough feedback or by withholding approval. Still, Berger’s teaching shows there’s a way to do it that actually empowers kids to do their best. View this post on Instagram Finally, it’s a great reminder that kids are capable of so much more than we give them credit for. Instead of accepting Austin’s drawing at face value and applauding his effort, Berger helped him make a stunning improvement with the right coaching. Berger began sharing Austin’s story around 2012, a few years after originally teaching Austin. It’s no wonder that such a powerful and insightful lesson is still being used to inspire people over a decade later. The post A first grader drew a butterfly. Then his classmates helped him see what he’d missed in the wings. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Το Τέξας σχεδιάζει κέντρο δεδομένων 60 MW με ψύξη κλειστού βρόχου και ταχύτερη κατασκευή
items.titleOriginal: Texas plans 60MW data center with closed-loop cooling and faster construction
items.description: Η Giga Energy ανακοίνωσε μια συμφωνία μίσθωσης 1 δισεκατομμυρίου δολαρίων με έναν άγνωστο πάροχο cloud τεχνητής νοημοσύνης με έδρα τις ΗΠΑ για την ανάπτυξη μιας πανεπιστημιούπολης κέντρου δεδομένων 60 μεγαβάτ (MW) στην κομητεία Χαντ του Τέξας. Η εγκατάσταση θα χρησιμοποιεί ένα σύστημα ψύξης κλειστού βρόχου που θα λειτουργεί χωρίς δημοτικά ή υπόγεια ύδατα για υπολογιστικές λειτουργίες. Ονομάζεται Project Clay, η κατασκευή περίπου 30 στρεμμάτων…
items.descriptionOriginal: Giga Energy has announced a $1 billion lease agreement with an undisclosed US-based AI cloud provider to develop a 60-megawatt (MW) data center campus in Hunt County, Texas. The facility will use a closed-loop cooling system that operates without municipal or groundwater for computing operations. Called Project Clay, the approximately 30-acre development is being built by Giga Energy, which will develop, own and operate the campus. The company broke ground in July and expects the facility to be ready for service in spring 2027. The project is designed to address growing concerns about the environmental and infrastructure demands of large-scale computing facilities. As demand for AI processing capacity rises, data center developers face increasing scrutiny over their electricity requirements, water consumption and impact on surrounding communities. Giga Energy says its new GigaBase system combines modular construction with dedicated electrical infrastructure and water-efficient cooling to reduce the burden on local resources. Closed-loop cooling cuts water demand Unlike conventional data center cooling systems that can rely on evaporative cooling, Project Clay will use a fully closed-loop system to cool its computing equipment. Giga Energy said the system operates independently of municipal and groundwater supplies. The only water consumption at the facility will be for employee facilities, including sinks and bathrooms. The company estimates this usage will be comparable to that of two homes annually. The development will also use dedicated electrical infrastructure that taps underutilized capacity in the county. Giga Energy said the arrangement is designed to prevent the facility from drawing on distribution capacity serving existing homes and businesses. Water and electricity consumption have become major considerations in data center development, particularly in regions facing resource constraints. Large computing facilities require substantial power to operate servers and cooling equipment, placing additional demands on local infrastructure. Giga Energy said Project Clay was designed to address these concerns while bringing new computing capacity to the region. Modular design speeds construction The company is using a factory-first construction approach for the project, manufacturing much of the facility off-site before assembling it at the Hunt County location. Giga Energy said this approach could reduce construction time to under eight months, less than half the time required for traditional builds. The modular approach is also expected to reduce truck traffic, road disruption and construction activity around nearby communities. The company said the GigaBase system is intended to make data center deployment faster while reducing pressure on local infrastructure. Project Clay is expected to create approximately 300 construction jobs during development and 24 permanent full-time positions. Giga Energy estimates annual salaries for the permanent roles will range from $116,000 to $180,000. The company also expects the campus to generate millions of dollars in recurring annual tax revenue for Hunt County. These funds could support local schools, public infrastructure, emergency services and other public needs, although Giga Energy has not disclosed a specific revenue estimate. The $1 billion lease agreement marks a major commitment to the facility, although the identity of the cloud provider has not been disclosed. As AI computing demand continues to expand, projects such as Project Clay highlight how developers are exploring modular construction, dedicated power infrastructure and closed-loop cooling to address the resource demands of data centers .

items.title: «Νόμιζα ότι ήμουν κακός στην τέχνη»: Πώς ένα μουσείο αλλάζει τον τρόπο με τον οποίο τα παιδιά βλέπουν τη δημιουργικότητά τους
items.titleOriginal: ‘I Thought I Was Bad at Art’: How a Museum Is Changing the Way Children See Their Creativity
items.description: «Ένιωσα ότι υπήρχαν ευκαιρίες να ζωγραφίσω και να συμμετάσχω σε σχολικές δραστηριότητες, αλλά υπήρχαν λιγότερες πιθανότητες για τα παιδιά να παρουσιάσουν τη δουλειά τους σε ένα ευρύτερο κοινό». Για τον 18χρονο Sahil Santosh Kundojwar, η τέχνη ήταν κάτι που του άρεσε να δημιουργεί, αλλά κυρίως το μοιραζόταν με δασκάλους, φίλους και οικογένεια. Είχε ευκαιρίες να ζωγραφίσει στο σχολείο, αλλά φι…
items.descriptionOriginal: "I felt that there were opportunities to draw and participate in school activities, but there were fewer chances for children to showcase their work to a wider audience." For 18-year-old Sahil Santosh Kundojwar, art was something he enjoyed creating but mostly shared with teachers, friends, and family. He had opportunities to draw at school, but finding an audience beyond his immediate circle was not easy. That changed in July 2024, when a teacher at The Aditya Birla Public School in Awarpur, Maharashtra, introduced him to the Children's Art Museum of India (CAMI). He submitted a drawing of Ganpati Bappa for a theme called 'My Superhero'. It won a prize, giving him the encouragement to share more of his work. "I didn't expect to win a prize, so receiving recognition for my Ganpati artwork was a very special and motivating experience for me," he says. His story reflects the idea behind CAMI, a digital museum that gives children a dedicated space to display their artwork. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, the platform has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. Its collection includes over 20,000 artworks, and the website has received more than a million visitors from over 200 towns and cities. The idea began with a question the siblings found themselves asking during COVID-19. Children were creating art at home, but where could they go to have it seen, appreciated, and preserved? A museum of their own During the pandemic, the siblings were spending more time at home and creating art themselves. They noticed that children around them were doing the same, but much of this work stayed in school notebooks, folders, or at home, with few opportunities to reach a wider audience. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, CAMI has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. They felt that children's artwork should not be limited to occasional displays at school exhibitions or relegated to a corner of a museum primarily meant for adults. They wanted to build a space where young artists would be at the centre. Krish recalls the question that set the idea in motion. "Why wasn't there a space where a child could say, 'This is my artwork, and it belongs in a museum'?" Krish, now 16 and a Class 11 student at The Shri Ram School in Gurugram, and Manya, 19, who is pursuing a bachelor's degree in the United States, began working on the idea together. For the 16-year-old, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. "I wanted to create a space where children could see their artwork displayed, feel that it mattered, and know that it deserved to be seen," he says. Manya wanted the experience to feel different from uploading an image online. "We did not want to create just another website where children could upload pictures. We wanted the artwork to have a context and a sense of recognition," she tells The Better India . Turning that idea into a functioning museum meant learning almost everything from scratch. The siblings began with an Excel spreadsheet, mapping out how children would submit their work and how the museum would organise and display it. They experimented with WordPress and Wix to build early versions of the website and emailed schools and children to gauge interest. There was no established organisation or technical team behind them. They learnt about website development, communication, curation, and outreach as they went along, with their parents helping them through the early stages. "The first step was deciding that we were going to build it rather than keep talking about it," Krish says. The website went live in January 2022. Its first version was uncomplicated, allowing children to submit artwork and have it displayed in an online collection. The first submission was a picture of a peacock sent in by a young child. Because the website did not yet require all the details it collects today, the founders knew very little about the artist. They have even tried to trace her since. Krish remembers the submission for what it represented. "There was just a child who had created something and wanted a place to share it," he says. Where young artists find recognition As children began finding the platform, CAMI grew beyond its original digital collection. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. One such initiative is the monthly ArtFest. Each edition revolves around a theme or creative prompt, which children can interpret in their own way before submitting their artwork. Selected entries are showcased as part of the programme. For Krish, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. The idea is to encourage participation rather than make creativity depend on winning a competition. Manya says the team wanted children to have opportunities to return to the platform and keep experimenting. "We realised that children should not have to wait for one opportunity to submit their artwork. We wanted our initiative to give them regular reasons to create, participate, and explore," she says. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries , ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. These programmes allow students to display their work beyond the classroom. Its collaborations include Sarvodaya schools in Delhi, the Aditya Birla Group, and Bagiya Foundation. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. Each entry goes through a verification process to ensure it is appropriate for children. Art teachers, curators, and members of the core team review submissions, generally within 24 to 48 hours. The team considers originality, effort, and creative expression rather than expecting professional-level technique. Accepted artwork becomes part of the digital collection or may be considered for an ArtFest, exhibition, or school gallery. Children also receive a CAMI certificate. "We are not looking for technical perfection. A child's artwork does not need to look professionally executed to have value," explains the teen founder. The museum has also developed a learning section with resources on creating, appreciating, and understanding different art forms. These include traditional and indigenous Indian styles such as Warli, Madhubani, and Pattachitra. Children and visitors can also engage with CAMI through its YouTube channel and Spotify podcast. In 2023, the founders took the museum into another digital environment by launching a virtual museum on Roblox. With more than 120 million daily active users globally, the platform offered a way to reach children in a space where they already play, create, and connect. The virtual museum allows players to walk through galleries and view artwork made by children. It has received over 2,70,600 visits, extending the reach of the collection beyond the conventional website. What recognition can mean to a young artist? For the founders, the value of the initiative is not measured only through membership figures or the number of artworks in its collection. Some of the most meaningful moments have come through the responses they receive from children. Manya remembers an Instagram message from a girl who was around 12. After seeing her painting displayed in the museum, the child wrote, "I used to think I wasn't good at art, but when you displayed my painting in the museum, I began to feel that maybe I was," she recalls. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. The message stayed with the co-founder because it showed how being taken seriously could change a child's perception of their own ability. "She was not suddenly a professional artist, and nothing about her artistic ability had changed overnight. What changed was that someone had taken her work seriously enough to give it a place," she says. Manya has also seen how children's creative expression changes as they continue making and sharing art. Some begin with familiar drawings of two mountains and the sun, but gradually experiment with portraits, posters, different compositions, and styles such as cubism and modern art. "For me, that progression is not really about becoming a 'better' artist in a technical sense. It is about becoming more confident in having an idea of their own and being willing to experiment with it," she says. Seventeen-year-old Kritika from Delhi has experienced some of that encouragement herself. Before joining CAMI in September this year, she mostly shared her artwork with family or during school art classes. She wanted to see her work displayed alongside that of other children and hoped for feedback that would help her take herself seriously as an artist. Her first submission, titled 'Fish Illusion', was accepted for the online gallery. Seeing it published encouraged her to begin working on another project. "When I first submitted my artwork on the website, I hoped that my work would be accepted and displayed on a real platform. I wanted to see how it looked alongside other children's art and hoped to get some encouragement or feedback that would make me feel like a real artist," she says. Her parents' response to the painting also stayed with her. They complimented her use of colours and told her that the artwork had brought a smile to their faces. "That made me realise that my art has the power to make people happy," she adds. Having her work displayed on the platform has made her more comfortable sharing it with others. "Now, I feel incredibly proud to show people my work and confidently call myself an artist," she says. Sahil, too, explains that the recognition he received through CAMI made him more confident about putting his work forward. Appreciation from teachers and classmates after winning the Monthly Best Prize encouraged him to participate in more activities. He has one piece of advice for young artists. "I would tell them not to be afraid or shy about showing their work. If you are proud of what you have created, you should share it with others because your creativity is special and unique . Don't worry about whether everyone will like it," he says. Building a community across India As the initiative developed its programmes, its reach began extending beyond the founders' immediate circles. What started with children from familiar schools and communities now includes participants from major cities as well as smaller towns and villages. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries, ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. The founders cite participation from places such as Vaniyambadi, Rampurhat, Guntur, Nainital, Khammam, Ranaghat, Patna, Bareilly, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Kanhagad, Prayagraj, Kota, and Puducherry. The platform has also reached villages in Uttarakhand and smaller communities in West Bengal and Odisha. Manya says the geographical spread has been one of the most surprising aspects of the journey. A digital museum, she explains, allows a child from a smaller town to participate in the same collection as someone living in a major city. The first major sign that CAMI was gaining momentum came by June 2022, when the team began receiving artwork submissions every day. Its first school collaboration showed the founders that they could reach groups of children through educators, rather than relying only on individual submissions. The Roblox museum, launched the following year, opened another route to young audiences. The initiative now has a core team of five members, supported by more than 20 volunteers and over 500 young brand ambassadors. It continues to operate as a bootstrapped initiative, with the founders relying on their own resources and family support rather than institutional venture funding. Their roles have changed as the museum has grown. Krish, who initially handled everything from the website and social media to school outreach and submissions, now focuses more on its development, operations, and future direction. Manya's responsibilities centre on ideation, marketing, outreach, and programme development. Building the initiative while studying has also taught them to manage their time and share responsibilities. Krish works on the initiative after school and during weekends, while prioritising academics during examinations. As the team has expanded, he has learnt to delegate rather than remain involved in every task. "I often say that school taught me how to learn, but CAMI taught me how to turn ideas into something real," he says. The siblings are now looking at ways to create more opportunities for young artists. These include exhibitions, local art initiatives led by ambassadors and avenues through which children can have their artwork commissioned. The co-founder sees this as a natural next step for a platform built around recognising young people's creativity. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. "If we tell children that their creative work has value, we should also think about how we can create real opportunities around that value," he says. From an Excel spreadsheet and a simple website to a community of more than 3 lakh registered members, CAMI has grown considerably since 2022. At its core, it continues to champion the idea that children's creativity deserves to be taken seriously , giving young artists the encouragement and recognition to keep creating. All pictures courtesy CAMI.

items.title: Η Lily Pad Pic κερδίζει το βραβείο Nature Photographer of the Year, μια «Σπάνια» Τιμή για την εικονογράφηση φυτών
items.titleOriginal: Lily Pad Pic Wins Nature Photographer of the Year Award, a “Rare” Honor for Plant Imagery
items.description: Ο φετινός διαγωνισμός Nature Photographer of the Year έλαβε 27.108 συμμετοχές από φωτογράφους σε περισσότερες από 96 χώρες — και ο γενικός νικητής, που ανακοινώθηκε στις 14 Νοεμβρίου, ξεχωρίζει με περισσότερους από έναν τρόπους. Με τίτλο «The One That Left and The One That Stayed», η φωτογραφία του Hannu Ahonen με ένα φύλλο νούφαρου δίπλα σε ένα παγωμένο αντίγραφο με εικόνα καθρέφτη είναι εκπληκτική στο i…
items.descriptionOriginal: This year’s Nature Photographer of the Year competition received 27,108 entries from photographers in more than 96 countries — and the overall winner, announced Nov. 14, stands out in more ways than one. Titled “The One That Left and the One That Stayed,” Hannu Ahonen’s shot of a water lily leaf beside a mirror-image frozen replica is stunning in its own right, but it’s also a “rare” example of a plant photo winning the annual contest, according to the chair of the judging panel, Theo Bosboom. “It is not often that a photograph of a plant is crowned the overall winner of a major photography competition, but the jury could not overlook this fascinating image by Hannu Ahonen,” Bosboom said in a press release shared with Nice News. “First and foremost, the photograph captures a unique situation: a water lily leaf with an almost perfect black-and-white replica of it lying next to it in the water.” He continued, “It takes a moment for the viewer to realize what has happened here: A thin layer of ice that had formed on the leaf has been blown away by the wind. The shapes in the sheet of ice are delicate; even the veins of the water lily leaf are clearly recognizable. Because the water lily and the sheet of ice are still touching, a sense of connection emerges; you realize that they belong together, like yin and yang.” In addition to being named overall winner, the Finnish photographer took the top spot in the Plants and Fungi category. Scroll on to see the other category winners and read commentary from the judging panel on each one. Birds: “Painting From the End of the World” by Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel (France) Lucas Mugnier-Lavorel / NPOTY 2026 “Environmental portraits of wildlife can make us feel closer to the animals despite being farther away from them, when done right. This image of a Magellanic woodpecker in its gorgeous habitat was a perfect example. It stood out from thousands of submissions because of its understated sense of place, beauty, simplicity, and timing. Diagonal lines formed by several trees guide the eyes to discover the bird — expertly framed against the backdrop and placed off-center — while encouraging exploration of the forest and the Patagonian landscape beyond it. Overall, it was a very successful reminder of how the portrayal of nature in its literal state can still be the most powerful of photographic expressions.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Mammals: “Play Misty” by Paul Goldstein (U.K.) Paul Goldstein / NPOTY 2026 “Quiet images can be easy to overlook in the fiercely competitive mammal category, one of the largest in NPOTY. This ethereal image of a giraffe peeking out of the mist revealed its strengths gradually. Initially a little disorienting, it offered just enough of a visual puzzle to keep the viewer engaged until the image resolved. The soft pastel colors create a soothing atmosphere, while the image’s simplicity and quiet emotion ultimately made it stand out among the category’s strongest contenders.” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Other Animals: “The Pitcher’s Micro Kingdom” by Marcus Kuan (Singapore) Marcus Kuan / NPOTY 2026 “The lighting, colors, and unexpected gathering of species immediately caught our attention. Kuan beautifully captured a world where crustaceans, amphibians, and carnivorous plants cross paths. As judges, we were drawn to the possibilities unfolding within this single frame. Could the pitchers be digesting invertebrates? Might the frog be exploring a potential egg-laying site, while the crab continues its daily search for food among the plants? The image invites us to imagine the separate lives of these organisms, briefly brought together. The carefully balanced composition, beautifully controlled lighting, and rich greens and reds against the dark nighttime background make this a striking photograph.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Landscape: “In the Circle of Vultures Around the Falls” by J Fritz Rumpf (U.S.) J Fritz Rumpf / NPOTY 2026 “What immediately caught our attention was the incredible light and atmosphere in this photo. The longer we looked, the more fascinating it became. There is so much to discover: the last light of day illuminating the mist rising from Iguazú Falls, the silhouettes of trees and rocks, the birds circling above, the sunlight streaming through an opening in the rock at the center, and the subtle waterfall on the left. The interplay of light and shadow transforms the immense power of the waterfalls into something intimate and almost dreamlike. A beautiful example of how an iconic natural wonder can be captured in a truly extraordinary way.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Underwater: “Beneath Aquatic Constellations” by Matt Pérez (U.S.) Matt Pérez / NPOTY 2026 “Pérez’s photograph immediately drew us in. As a jury, we wanted to linger over it, exploring the details and wondering what we were seeing. Newt egg masses decorate the submerged branches like baubles on a Christmas tree, framing the scene and guiding our eyes towards the pond turtle with its piercing yellow eyes.The scene feels almost otherworldly, busy with intricate details yet still peaceful to look at — an impressive balance to capture in a single photograph. Its beautiful composition, striking lighting, and balance of rich detail and serene feel made this photo stand out to the jury. Matt Pérez also deserves credit for stepping back from the turtles’ courtship behavior to capture this wider view of a male pond turtle within an extraordinary habitat.” – Jury member Louis Guillot Nature Art: “Peach Blossoms in the Snow” by Xuzhong Liu (China) Xuzhong Liu / NPOTY 2026 “This photograph has everything that can make a drone shot interesting and fascinating. First and foremost, there are beautiful shapes and subtle colors, but there is also a sense of alienation. What am I actually looking at, and what is the scale of the landscape in the photograph? The image was taken in September in a wetland area in China, but it reminded the photographer himself of peach blossoms he had previously photographed during a spring trip to Tibet. A good abstract photograph like this also leaves plenty of room for the viewer to decide for themselves what they see in it. This makes it the perfect winner of the nature art category.” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Human and Nature: “Evolution” by Petr Bambousek (Czechia) Petr Bambousek / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its striking depiction of the impact human activity has on local wildlife. The sleeping Malayan sun bear inside a garbage incinerator creates a powerful visual contrast, showing how habitat loss and human waste increasingly force wild animals into close contact with human environments. The image is both unexpected and unsettling, capturing a broader story of how wildlife is forced to adapt as its natural surroundings are altered and destroyed.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Black and White: “Storm on the Sea” by László Tóth (Hungary) László Tóth / NPOTY 2026 “This photo really stood out to us. At first, we were not quite sure what we were looking at. It sparked some wonderful discussions among the jury and made us look even closer. The black-and-white contrast, dark diagonal lines, and striking patterns create a fascinating abstract composition. It looks like a storm at sea, but in reality, it is a thin layer of snow shaped by strong winds on a frozen lake, captured from above.” – Jury member Ilse Koks Animal Portraits: “A Seal’s Worst Nightmare” by Audun Rikardsen (Norway) Audun Rikardsen / NPOTY 2026 “Just when we thought we had seen about every kind of polar bear image there is, along comes this shot taken from inside a hole in the ice looking up at the bear. Once you realize what is happening, you start thinking about how this shot could possibly have been taken. Then it dawns on you that it seems almost impossible, no matter how. Showing something never seen before is a pretty effective method of captivating an audience, and one that carried this image all the way to the top. With oceans warming and ice melting, the ‘What’s going on down there?’ look gives the image a deeper layer of meaning that I appreciate. Right now humanity is looking back up at the bear and shrugging its collective shoulders in pretense. For how much longer?” – Jury member Steffen Foerster Nature of “De Lage Landen”: “Fairies” by Enikő Kálovics (Hungary) Enikő Kálovics / NPOTY 2026 “The winning image stood out for its ability to transform a familiar landscape into something dreamlike and unexpected. The combination of the tiny lacewings, the autumn forest, and the purplish night sky creates a delicate, atmospheric interpretation of the nature of ‘De Lage Landen.’ The thoughtful use of double exposure adds another layer to the image, capturing not just the insects themselves, but also the sense of wonder and atmosphere of their natural habitat.” – Jury member Lana Tannir Fred Hazelhoff Award, Portfolio: “Eagle Owls in the City” by Simone Baumeister (Germany) Simone Baumeister / NPOTY 2026 “In the portfolio category, the bar is set considerably higher for participating photographers than in the individual categories. Whilst a single fantastic photograph is sufficient there, in the portfolio category you need a whole series of outstanding images that not only complement one another but also fit together well in terms of style and theme. Simone Baumeister has succeeded brilliantly in this with her portfolio on eagle owls in the city. It is clear that she has put a great deal of time into creating the series: She has managed to capture all sorts of special moments with her camera, and the series showcases a wide range of situations, locations, and atmospheres. In doing so, she offers a unique glimpse into the world of a bird that is making a comeback in Germany and which, despite its size, often goes unnoticed by the people around it. Or, as the photographer herself puts it, her images make the invisible visible. And that is one of the great strengths of (nature) photography!” – Judging panel chair Theo Bosboom Youth Photographer of the Year: “Tree of Life” by Parham Pourahmad (U.S.) Parham Pourahmad / NPOTY 2026 “In ‘Tree of Life,’ Pourahmad captured a striking scene that could comfortably hold its own in the adult categories. Black and white was an excellent choice, defining the coyote’s silhouette and revealing the majestic oak’s intricate network of branches. Even within this wider scene, the coyote’s downward gaze is clear. Pourahmad explained that it was searching for rodent prey, a small detail that brings the photograph to life. The image combines a beautiful portrait of the animal’s habitat with an intimate glimpse of its hunting behavior.” – Jury member Louis Guillot

items.title: Η μείωση του αριθμού των αστέγων στις ΗΠΑ σημειώνει την πιο απότομη πτώση του ενός έτους της τελευταίας δεκαετίας
items.titleOriginal: US homelessness decline hits its steepest one-year drop in a decade
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ ΟΠΤΙΜΙΣΤΩΝ Οι άστεγοι στις Ηνωμένες Πολιτείες μειώθηκαν κατά περισσότερο από έξι τοις εκατό το 2025, η πιο απότομη μείωση των αστέγων σε διάστημα ενός έτους σε περισσότερο από μια δεκαετία, η οποία οδηγεί σε περίπου 49.000 λιγότερους ανθρώπους χωρίς στέγη. Ήταν η δεύτερη συνεχόμενη ετήσια πτώση μετά από μια μικρότερη πτώση το 2024 και σπάει μια σειρά αυξήσεων που είχε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Homelessness in the United States fell by more than six percent in 2025, the steepest one-year homelessness decline in more than a decade, which works out to roughly 49,000 fewer people without housing. It was the second straight annual drop after a smaller dip in 2024, and it breaks a run of increases that had pushed the homeless population to record levels. The numbers come from the annual count conducted in communities nationwide. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) announced the results ahead of its detailed report, and a separate analysis of the same count , commissioned by the National Alliance to End Homelessness, found a similar decline. However, the two part ways on the question of why. Where the homelessness decline showed up Veterans and the long view The clearest long-term gains are among veterans. Homelessness among U.S. veterans dropped more than seven percent last year and is down nearly 60 percent since 2010. Ann Oliva, CEO of the alliance, ties that record to programs that move people off the street and into housing without preconditions. “Investments in programs like that are much closer to the scale of need for veterans than for any other population experiencing homelessness,” she said. Four big cities and two disaster zones A large share of the drop is concentrated in a handful of places. New York, Chicago, Boston and Denver all saw large numbers of asylum seekers arrive at their shelters during the Biden administration, and according to Devon Kurtz, public safety policy director at the Cicero Institute, a think tank aligned with the administration on homelessness policy, those cities now account for about half of the most recent decline. “That’s also the four cities that have driven half of the drop most recently,” he said. Kurtz also pointed to San Francisco, which is moving toward more sober-living housing that prohibits drugs and alcohol. Numbers also fell in western North Carolina and Hawaii, both hit by major weather disasters. When HUD and other agencies arrive to help displaced residents, people who were already unhoused often receive assistance they had not been getting before. Rents easing in some markets Oliva described the decline as broad and likely the result of several forces at once, including softer rental markets in parts of the country. Rents remain high, but they have come down from their pandemic peaks, which could slow the number of people losing housing for the first time. Competing explanations for falling homelessness The administration credits enforcement and recovery HUD Secretary Scott Turner attributed the decline to the administration’s broader agenda. HUD also cited stepped-up enforcement against encampments following the 2024 Supreme Court ruling that allowed cities to ban sleeping and camping in public places. The administration argues that the long-standing federal approach of placing people in permanent housing first and offering voluntary treatment afterward has failed, and it blames that approach for the rise in homelessness during the pandemic. Requiring residents to stay drug-free, it says, helps more people reach recovery. HUD wants to redirect several billion dollars in homelessness funding toward short-term housing paired with mandatory addiction and mental health treatment, a plan courts have blocked so far. Advocates credit housing programs The alliance reads the same data differently. “It’s good news that more people are getting housed, and that the programs that are funded by Congress are working,” Oliva said. She argued that housing-first programs were a major driver of the decline, particularly for veterans , and said the analysis her group commissioned found that cities with camping bans performed worse than the national average. Critics of drug-free housing requirements add that relapse is common, and that such rules can push people back onto the street when it happens. The work still ahead Chronic homelessness moved the other way Both analyses agree that nearly 700,000 people in the U.S. are still living in shelters or on the streets, well above pre-pandemic levels. One group also bucked the trend: people who have been homeless for a long time saw a small increase last year, even as most other groups declined. Oliva said this population, which is more likely to live with mental illness and addiction , needs more permanent housing, while the administration is pushing for treatment-linked short-term options. With HUD’s funding overhaul still tied up in court, the next annual count will show whether the homelessness decline holds, and how far either approach can reach the people who have been without a home the longest. items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Αυτό το άρθρο είναι μέρος της σειράς Local Changemakers 2026 του The Optimist Daily, δίνοντας έμφαση στους δημιουργούς αλλαγής 30 ετών και κάτω. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Most public spaces are built for an average visitor who doesn’t exist. The lighting, the noise, the textures underfoot, and the pace of a room all assume a certain kind of body and brain, and anyone who takes in the world differently is left to manage on their own. April Surac, a Florida teenager and the founder of NeuraSensa , has spent the past two years making the opposite: art that changes in response to whoever is standing in front of it. How NeuraSensa began in a furniture workshop Textures, materials and a younger sister April grew up in her family’s furniture workshop, where she learned early that materials follow their own logic and that a texture one person finds soothing can be unbearable to someone else. She also grew up with a younger sister who has autism , and that taught her something before she had words for it: the designed world fits some nervous systems far better than others. Paul Moore, who nominated April for this series and has followed the project since the beginning, sees both influences running through everything she makes. “April is one of those students whose work has grown directly out of something deeply personal to her,” he said. April founded NeuraSensa in June 2024, and she has summed up its guiding idea in a single sentence: “I believe design should adapt to people, not the other way around.” NeuraSensa’s responsive textile installations Art that reacts to touch, motion, light and sound The installations layer fabric with embedded sensors, so surfaces shift under a visitor’s hand and the light and sound in the room change as people move through it. For someone whose senses register the world at a different intensity, a space that responds instead of making fixed demands can decide whether they stay or leave. NeuraSensa designs this work for autistic people and others with sensory or cognitive differences, including people living with dementia. The installations have reached more than 15,000 people through gallery exhibitions and community events, with shows at SOBO Windermere Art Gallery and CityArts Orlando. NeuraSensa has also run workshops with organizations such as United Cerebral Palsy of Central Florida and the Brevard Achievement Center , where participants work hands-on with April’s sensory-friendly pieces. Sensory kits for homes, classrooms and hospitals Outside the gallery, NeuraSensa’s Sponsor-a-Kit program has distributed more than 250 therapeutic kits to families, educators, hospitals and disability-serving organizations, putting sensory support tools into places that rarely have them. April also organized a community drive that delivered more than $3,000 worth of tactile toys to Nemours Children’s Hospital in Orlando. Much of this runs on her own resources. She funds NeuraSensa through personal savings, grants, and fundraising, and Moore has watched how much that asks of her. “I have seen firsthand how much of her own time, savings, grant funding and effort she puts into making each project possible,” he said. A young changemaker’s growing recognition The Barron Prize and a TEDx stage In 2025, April was one of 15 top winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes , each of whom receives $10,000 toward their work or education. That same year, she was named a Daily Point of Light honoree by the Points of Light organization, and she has since been nominated for the KidsRights international award and published research through Figshare. According to Moore, she gave a TED-Ed Talk in October titled “ What’s Next: Designing Technology for Every Nervous System ,” which he said she developed with mentorship from a Nobel laureate in neuroscience. “I’ve loved seeing her share each stage of that journey with me, and watching an idea close to her heart grow into work that has now supported thousands of people in our community,” Moore wrote. Sensory-inclusive design beyond compliance From retrofits to spaces built for everyone For a long time, making public space accessible meant meeting minimum requirements after a building or exhibit was already finished. The conversation around neurodivergence in art and public life has moved toward design justice, the principle that spaces should be planned from the start for the full range of human experience instead of patched later for people who fall outside a narrow norm. NeuraSensa sits where art practice and disability advocacy overlap, and April has not waited for museums or city planners to adopt that principle before acting on it. The next phase reaches well past Central Florida. April is developing commissions for galleries in New York City, Los Angeles and London, along with textile-based systems for large installations and wearable sensory tools, designs she is moving toward patent protection. Moore says he is “incredibly proud of how she keeps learning, expanding the project and finding new ways to use her talents in service of others,” and the scale of what she’s attempting suggests the lesson from her family’s workshop has traveled a long way: a room can be built to meet the person who walks into it, wherever that room turns out to be. You can follow her work on NeuraSensa’s Instagram . Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.titleOriginal: Two strangers stranded at El Paso airport take epic leap of faith in 12-hour road trip together
items.description: Τα αεροπορικά ταξίδια δεν πηγαίνουν πάντα όπως τα σχεδιάζετε. Αυτό ίσχυε ιδιαίτερα το περασμένο Σαββατοκύριακο, καθώς η FAA καθήλωσε άνευ προηγουμένου χιλιάδες αεροπλάνα, ακυρώνοντας και καθυστερώντας πτήσεις και προκαλώντας πραγματικά όλεθρο στους ταξιδιώτες. Οι λόγοι πίσω από το κλείσιμο εξακολουθούν να διευκρινίζονται στα παρασκήνια. Αλλά αυτή η ιστορία δεν αφορά αυτό. Αντίθετα, είναι η ιστορία…
items.descriptionOriginal: Air travel doesn’t always go as planned. That was especially true this past weekend, as the FAA unprecedentedly grounded thousands of planes, canceling and delaying flights and genuinely wreaking havoc on travelers. The reasons behind the shutdown are still being sorted out behind the scenes. But this story isn’t about that. Instead, it’s the tale of what could have been an extremely negative situation and how the butterfly effect changed lives. This was the case for at least two travelers, who turned the lemon-like circumstance into the refreshing start of a new friendship. An Instagram video posted by NBC LA News begins with a blonde woman making a bold statement: “I don’t want to say that the universe shut down aviation just so Michelle and I could become friends,” she declares. A chyron over the clip reads, “A friendship takes flight after the FAA ground stop.” View this post on Instagram Things started to get weird NBC LA Journalist Karma Dickerson explains, “Nikki Chambers was waiting to board her flight from El Paso Friday afternoon, when things started to get weird.” The clip bounces back to Chambers, who shares how odd things had begun to get at the airport. “And it even said ‘flight left’ on the screen, and I’m like, ‘No, it didn’t! We’re still here.’” She laughs and rolls her eyes. “So it seemed really eerie.” Dickerson continues, “Michelle Navarro was sitting nearby, noting the same.” We then see Navarro, who’s listed only as “traveler,” share with the news outlet how it all went down. “There was an influx of law enforcement and dogs. And they were running the dogs,” she explained. The two women got to chatting The two women began chatting, Dickerson explains. Chambers continues, “I go, ‘Where do you live?’ She said Westminster. And I’m like, ‘I’m in Huntington!’” Quite some time later, they made a decision. Dickerson shares, “Four hours into the nationwide ground stop and their in-depth convo, they called it. It was time for a new plan. With all the uncertainty, Nikki felt safer on the ground. And Michelle? She had somewhere to be.” Navarro then reveals that that day was actually quite special. She tells Dickerson, “Today was my wedding shower!” We then flash to a photo of Navarro surrounded by friends at a restaurant wearing a wedding veil. Dickerson laughs, reporting, “As you might have guessed, she made it. Thanks to a 12-hour car ride with a stranger.” Navarro jokes, “She didn’t look like a serial killer, so I was like, ‘Alright, let’s do this!’” A decision based on snacks The video cuts back to Chambers, who explains what ultimately led her to trust her new friend. “She pulled out this little tray of snacks that her fiancé had made for her, with all kinds of little nibblies in it. And she offered me some. And at that moment, I’m like, I’m getting in a van with this lady, aren’t I? She’s got good snacks!” We then see a photo of two women making peace signs in comfy clothes as they embark on their road adventure. The reporter relays, “So the two Orange County women set out at 7:00 a.m., their rented car upgraded to a minivan, turning what could have been a brutal 800-mile trek into an impromptu great American road trip.” Wedding plans Chambers explains, “By about mid-trip, she’s like, ‘Do you want to come to the wedding?’” She covers her mouth and then flashes a huge smile. “I’m like, ‘Yes!’” Wrapping up the story, Dickerson shares, “So at the very least, we know Michelle and Nikki will be meeting again once more. Though both women tell me they suspect that, as they embark on their next life adventures, they’ll be doing it with a new friend along for the ride.” The story delighted many Instagrammers and inspired them, too. One writes, “Next, you will find them using this in their airline campaigns. ‘Flight canceled? Hang out in one of our restaurants and make a friend.’” Another points out that this is a sure sign that adults can make friends as easily as we did in childhood. “So often we lament it’s too bad we can’t just make friends as easily as we did in kindergarten and here these women are, proving it’s still possible to get by on proximity, vibes, and snacks.” Yet another shares what many Gen Xers might have been thinking: “It’s giving Planes, Trains, and Automobiles lol, convenient movie for the holiday month.” The post Two strangers stranded at El Paso airport take epic leap of faith in 12-hour road trip together appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire.
items.description: Τις πρώτες πρωινές ώρες της 30ης Απριλίου 1994, ο Joe Campbell πήγε στον τηλεφωνικό θάλαμο κοντά στο σπίτι του στο Forest Gate, στο Ανατολικό Λονδίνο, για να τηλεφωνήσει στους γονείς του στη Γουιάνα. Στην αρχή, σκέφτηκε ότι υπήρχε μια πεταμένη σακούλα με πατατάκια μέσα. Ήταν ένα νεογέννητο κορίτσι, περίπου δύο ωρών, με τον ομφάλιο λώρο του ακόμα συνδεδεμένο. Ο Κάμπελ κάλεσε το 999 (η βρετανική έκδοση του 911) α…
items.descriptionOriginal: In the early hours of April 30, 1994, Joe Campbell walked to the phone booth near his home in Forest Gate, East London , to call his parents in Guyana. At first, he thought there was a discarded bag of chips inside. It was a newborn girl, about two hours old, with her umbilical cord still attached. Campbell called 999 (the British version of 911) and stayed with her until help arrived. He asked if he could adopt her, but he was told no, in part because he wasn’t married. But he gave her the name “April,” and for years he sent her birthday cards and presents until social services eventually asked him to stop. She was adopted by another family when she was 3. She grew up knowing almost nothing about the man who found her until 2016, at age 22, she made a public appeal in the London newspaper Metro to find him. A colleague at the delivery company where Campbell worked saw it and showed him. View this post on Instagram “I ran home and [told] my daughter Rihanna on the phone, ‘I think I found April,’” Campbell recalled on Good Morning Britain . They reunited that summer, and they’ve been family ever since. She changed her name to April, and she calls him Dad. View this post on Instagram “Joe is complete family,” she said, according to SWNS . “His kids are my siblings now. We’re so close, we stay at each other’s houses. He never stopped thinking about me. I don’t know what this man is. An angel.” Campbell is now 62 and still drives a bus. So April, a bank employee in West London, has started a fundraiser to help him retire early. The pair went back on Good Morning Britain in October to talk about the decade since their reunion. The post A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Οι Βρετανοί παππούδες δοκιμάζουν για πρώτη φορά το «Minnesota sushi», το «puppy chow» και άλλα κλασικά Midwestern
items.titleOriginal: British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time
items.description: Στο κανάλι τους στο JOLLY YouTube, οι δημιουργοί περιεχομένου Josh και Ollie κάνουν κάθε είδους διασκεδαστικά πειράματα πολιτιστικής σύγκρουσης με φαγητό . Πρόσφατα αποφάσισαν να δουν τι θα έφτιαχναν οι Βρετανοί παππούδες, ή «αποφυγές του φέρετρου», όπως περιέγραψαν τους εαυτούς τους, από κάποιο κλασικό φαγητό της Midwestern. Η μεσοδυτική κουζίνα τείνει να ευνοεί το χορταστικό, χορταστικό φαγητό με άφθονο…
items.descriptionOriginal: On their JOLLY YouTube channel, content creators Josh and Ollie do all kinds of fun culture-clash experiments featuring food . They recently decided to see what British grandparents, or “coffin dodgers,” as they described themselves, would make of some classic Midwestern comfort food. Midwestern cuisine tends to favor hearty, filling food with plenty of casseroles (also known as hotdishes), creamy sauces, and generous helpings of meat, cheese, and potatoes. Much of the region’s food traditions were shaped by European immigrants, particularly Germans and Scandinavians, as well as the ingredients and practical cooking styles that became common across the Midwest. That might sound pretty familiar to a British palate. British cuisine has its own long history of hearty meals built around meat, potatoes, vegetables, gravy, and other comforting staples. But familiar ingredients don’t always make for familiar dishes. These grandparents’ reactions prove just how much room there is for cultural confusion at the dinner table. First up were the appetizers, which included ranch dressing with vegetables, cheese curds, and “Minnesota sushi” Thanks to the World Cup , many non-Americans were introduced to ranch and became instantly obsessed, with some even trying to smuggle or ship it back home. This time around, the condiment was equally well received. The grandparents described it as “ubiquitous” and “cheeky but not flippant,” which is both hilarious and, somehow, a pretty good description of ranch. “Minnesota sushi,” on the other hand, required a little more explanation. Despite its name, it contains no fish, rice, or seaweed. Instead, softened cream cheese and a pickle are rolled up in deli meat and sliced into little pinwheels. The grandparents weren’t quite as enthusiastic about this one, though it earned praise for its “nice crunch” and for being “non-threatening.” Cheese curds were another story. Josh and Ollie dubbed them “prepubescent cheese,” referring to the fact that cheese curds are the solid chunks of milk that eventually become cheese. Despite the slightly alarming name, they went over pretty well. Moving on to the main course: meatloaf, taco salad, and tater tot casserole Meatloaf got off to a slightly rocky start when it was compared to an elephant’s foot and even the radioactive runoff from the Chernobyl disaster. But apparently, appearances weren’t everything. Despite the unflattering comparisons, the grandparents declared it “delicious” and “proper English men’s food.” Tater tot casserole, more often called hotdishes among Midwesterners, is often made with a layer of seasoned ground meat, some veggies, and melted cheese. And of course, a crowning layer of crispy tater tots. This was a bit of a two-for-one discovery, as the hosts had to first explain what a tater tot was. A typical tater tot casserole. Photo credit: Canva The taco salad was also a hit, even if they did pronounce it “tah-co” salad. This dish has an interesting American history, too. According to The New York Times , the taco salad got its start at Disneyland’s Casa de Fritos restaurant in 1955, where staff created an edible corn-chip cup called the “Ta-Cup.” Finally, dessert: if peanut butter can be added, peanut butter will be added As one viewer put it, “The thing about the Midwest is, if we can slap peanut butter into a dessert, by thunder we will.” The desserts in question were Puppy Chow (also known as Muddy Buddies), made with crispy cereal coated in melted chocolate and peanut butter and tossed in powdered sugar, and Scotcheroos, which combines a chewy peanut butter-and-crispy rice-cereal base with melted chocolate and butterscotch. A bowl of Puppy Chow. Photo credit: Canva And to wash it all down, the Brits had Faygo and root beer The grandparents found Faygo “too sweet” and “undrinkable,” and root beer seemed to taste medicinal. That can be chalked up to its distinctive wintergreen flavor, which is used in many mouthwashes, dental rinses, and toothpastes in Britain. For the most part, the grandparents seemed to enjoy their tour through Midwestern cuisine. Some dishes earned immediate approval, while others required a little more convincing. But the food wasn’t quite the best part of the video. At the end, Josh and Ollie asked their taste testers to share a little life advice. The grandparents offered wonderfully simple answers. Here are some of the best nuggets: “Have lots of fun.” “Make the most of every day.” “Don’t take yourself too seriously.” “Be kind and love people.” “Whatever dream you have, go for it.” “Never stop learning.” While we may have different opinions on root beer and “prepubescent cheese,” we can agree on their advice, no matter which side of the pond we hail from. Follow JOLLY on YouTube for even more delicious and delightful food reviews. The post British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Μια μελέτη με παιδιά της δεκαετίας του '90 διαπίστωσε ότι τα τακτικά ταξίδια στο πάρκο συνδέονται με 17% καλύτερη ψυχική υγεία
items.titleOriginal: A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health
items.description: Δεν είναι μυστικό ότι τα smartphone, το YouTube και τα iPad έχουν αλλάξει δραματικά την παιδική ηλικία για τα Gen Z και Gen Alpha. Από τότε που εμφανίστηκαν τα smartphone και τα iPad, τα παιδιά πέρασαν πολύ λιγότερο χρόνο σε εξωτερικούς χώρους. Το 2009, το 7% των παιδιών ηλικίας 6 έως 17 ετών πέρασαν μία ώρα ή λιγότερο στη φύση. Το 2025, ο αριθμός αυτός έχει υπερτετραπλασιαστεί σε 26%. Ένα νέο καρφί…
items.descriptionOriginal: It’s no secret that smartphones, YouTube, and iPads have dramatically changed what childhood looks like for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Since smartphones and iPads came on the scene, kids have spent far less time outdoors. In 2009, 7% of children ages 6 to 17 spent an hour or less in nature. In 2025, that number has more than quadrupled to 26%. A new study from the University of Exeter shows why it’s so important for kids to spend plenty of time outside, especially when they’re playing with others. Researchers found that children who grew up in the ‘90s and visited a park at least once a week scored 16.5% better on mental health assessments than those who did not. Kids running on the playground. Photo credit: Canva The study used data from the Children of the 90s long-term cohort study. The study recruited more than 14,000 pregnant women from April 1991 to December 1992 and followed their children extensively for decades. Taking children to parks is great for their mental health “Our research suggests encouraging children to visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week could be a practical way to support their emotional wellbeing, social skills and mental health. But for this to work fairly, communities need good-quality parks that are safe, accessible and welcoming to families from all backgrounds,” lead researcher Mark Ferguson of the University of Exeter said in a statement . “Parks give children space to be physically active, which is known to support mental and physical health, as well as helping adventurous and imaginative play to build confidence and independence. We believe parks could be more than places to play, but an important resource for children’s healthy development,” Ferguson continued. Play equipment from the ’90s. Photo credit: Canva The study comes at a time when there has been a sharp increase in mental health disorders among children and teens. According to the 2026 Health of Women and Children Report , nearly 12.4 million American children had a diagnosed mental health condition in 2023- 2024, approximately 3 million more than in 2016-2017. Parks are a great place for strengthening mental health When children spend time at a park, they learn to make new friends, persevere through a tough run on the monkey bars, and use their imaginations. This supports their social-emotional development and helps them handle everyday challenges. Building a strong foundation of social-emotional development lays the groundwork for good mental health in childhood and beyond. A young girl with an iPad. Photo credit: Canva The researchers also found an interesting tidbit about children’s socioeconomic backgrounds. Young children born into more affluent families spend more time in parks than socioeconomically disadvantaged children. But as they get older, the pattern shifts: advantaged children go to the park less than disadvantaged children. The study is a great reminder of how important it is for kids to get out and play at their local parks. It’s also a call for communities to set aside ample space for parks and recreation areas and ensure they are safe and well staffed. As the study shows, going to the park isn’t just about an afternoon of fun for a child, but a lifetime of improved mental health. The post A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health appeared first on Upworthy .

items.description: Ο Sonny Gallardo, 14, και η οικογένειά του βγήκαν έξω από το χωριό Prairie Village του Κάνσας, το σπίτι τους το Halloween σε μια συγκλονιστική ανακάλυψη: ο πολύτιμος (και ακριβός) εξοπλισμός περιποίησης του γκαζόν του είχε κλαπεί μέσα σε μια νύχτα. "Ξύπνησα και η γιαγιά μου είπε ότι μας έκλεψαν τον εξοπλισμό. Βγήκα έξω και είχε [φύγει]", λέει ο Gallardo στο Upworthy. «Δεν το πίστευα στην αρχή.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sonny Gallardo, 14, and his family stepped outside their Prairie Village, Kansas, home on Halloween to a shocking discovery: his precious (and pricey) lawn care equipment had been stolen overnight. “I woke up, and my grandma said our equipment got stolen. I walked outside, and it was [gone],” Gallardo tells Upworthy. “I didn’t believe it at first. I still don’t. We assumed it was safe.” The ninth-grader and his family, who founded his lawn-mowing and lawn-care business named Sunnyside Jobs, LLC, went to the police station to file a report. What happened next has left them shocked, humbled, and grateful. View this post on Instagram Gallardo’s lawn care business beginnings Gallardo started mowing lawns when he was just 10 years old. “I know how it feels to walk outside to a nice lawn,” he tells Upworthy. “It brings other people joy.” With the help of his grandma Monica, his grandpa, two friends, and his aunt (who handles administrative work), the business expanded to offer power washing, leaf and junk removal, and more. “We do everything,” Gallardo adds. “It’s fun. I just really like doing it. It’s satisfying to me, and [we mow] about 30-35 lawns.” So when his equipment—including a 10-foot trailer with five lawn mowers on it, totaling over $20,000—was stolen, he was devastated. Until his community and kind strangers rallied around him. Donations flood in for Gallardo Gallardo’s grandmother started a GoFundMe to help cover the costs of the arduous process of buying back his lawn-care equipment. “They also cleared out everything from the back of the work vehicle,” she wrote. “Everything Sonny has worked so hard for was gone in minutes. Sonny was completely devastated, and so is the family.” Unfortunately, Gallardo was in the process of securing insurance for his newly formed LLC—but “coverage was not yet in place.” Within the first day or two, they raised about $600 toward a $20,000 goal. That’s when a local Kansas City news station learned about Gallardo’s situation. With their coverage, the GoFundMe goal was exceeded within weeks. Today, kind strangers have donated nearly $35,000 to help re-establish his business. “It’s crazy. It’s been a lot of support, especially from the lawn mowing community,” Gallardo tells Upworthy. “They’ve donated a lot of lawn equipment. I’m still doing lawns and leaf pickup.” His grandmother credits Sonny with being fiscally responsible, noting that he had enough saved to buy a new lawn mower in the interim. “We’ve been receiving all of these blessings. It’s overwhelming,” she tells Upworthy. With the funds, Gallardo plans to grow his business. “We’re for sure going to expand and have more crews out there,” he shared. Nearly 900 people have donated and left hopeful, personal notes for Gallardo and his family. “You’re inspiring young man, and don’t lose heart from this setback. Keep your spirits up!” one wrote. Another added, “You are an inspirational and determined young man, you will always succeed with such attributes. Peace & blessings.” The post Thieves stole 14-year-old’s lawn care business equipment. Kind strangers donated $37,000 to help. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Feel-Good τηλεοπτικά αγαπημένα: 30 σειρές ροής που θα φωτίσουν την ημέρα σας
items.titleOriginal: Feel-Good TV Favorites: 30 Streaming Shows That’ll Brighten Your Day
items.description: Ποια είναι η συνταγή για μια καλή τηλεοπτική εκπομπή; Για κάποιους, είναι ένας συνδυασμός ρομαντισμού και χιούμορ. Για άλλους, είναι μια νοσταλγική ιστορία με συγγενείς χαρακτήρες. Και μερικές φορές συμβαίνει ακριβώς το αντίθετο: ριάλιτι απόδρασης που σε μεταφέρει κάπου μακριά. Ευτυχώς, οι ενθουσιώδεις ιστορίες όλων των ειδών είναι διαθέσιμες για ροή όλες τις ώρες της ημέρας (και της νύχτας).…
items.descriptionOriginal: What’s the recipe for a feel-good TV show? For some, it’s a mix of romance and humor. For others, it’s a nostalgic storyline with relatable characters. And sometimes it’s just the opposite: escapism reality TV that transports you somewhere far away. Luckily, uplifting stories of all kinds are available to stream at all hours of the day (and night). From comedies and coming-of-age-stories to heartwarming reality series, these shows can help you feel a little better about the world. So, make yourself a cup of tea and cozy up on the couch — a heartwarming streaming session awaits! A Man on the Inside | Netflix This is perhaps the most wholesome whodunit you’ll ever watch. In Season One, retired professor Charles (Ted Danson) goes undercover at a retirement community to investigate the theft of a family heirloom. The next season, he takes on a new case at a college campus where he meets Mona, played by Danson’s real-life wife of over 30 years, Mary Steenburgen. We’re excited to see what’s in store for Season Three, which, alas, will be this endearing tale’s final chapter . Abbott Elementary | Hulu This hilarious mockumentary series follows teachers (and an outrageous principal) at a Philadelphia public school who go above and beyond to help their students succeed, despite the hurdles the faculty encounters both in and out of the classroom. Fun fact: Abbott Elementary is named after Joyce Abbott , a real sixth-grade teacher who taught creator and star Quinta Brunson at Andrew Hamilton School in Philadelphia. All Creatures Great and Small | PBS and Prime Video All Creatures Great and Small is based on author and veterinarian James Herriot’s beloved memoirs about his years treating animals in rural Yorkshire beginning in the 1930s. The British series is so peaceful that all six seasons feel like taking a breath of fresh air (the seventh premieres in the U.S. in January 2027). Black-ish | Hulu This Emmy-winning comedy is heartwarming, family-centered, and will keep you laughing. Follow the beloved Johnsons for eight seasons as they navigate highs, lows, and life changes together. Choir | Disney+ Meet the inspiring kids who make up the Detroit Youth Choir (of America’s Got Talent fame ) in this moving Disney+ docuseries. Over six episodes, you’ll find yourself cheering on all of the talented singers as they pursue their dreams and prepare for “the performance of a lifetime”: taking the stage at Carnegie Hall in New York City. Derry Girls | Netflix Witty and wonderful, Derry Girls is a British teen sitcom that follows a tight-knit group of friends during “ The Troubles ” in Ireland. It’s a beautiful example of the power of embracing humor amid hardships, without glossing over truths. English Teacher | Hulu English Teacher is another warmhearted, witty comedy set in the classroom, and often the faculty lounge and principal’s office as well. You’ll follow a group of offbeat high school teachers in Austin, Texas, as they navigate everything from a chaotic camping trip to AI-powered trash cans. The show boasts a rating of 94% on Rotten Tomatoes, and our only complaint is that the episodes, which run just over 20 minutes, aren’t longer — because the characters are endlessly fun to be around. Extraordinary Attorney Woo | Netflix South Korean series Extraordinary Attorney Woo follows a young lawyer who is on the autism spectrum as she navigates everyday interactions in her unique and authentic way. The show, which is dubbed in English, has a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes and was the most-viewed title on Netflix for a week . Gilmore Girls | Hulu For a dose of mother-daughter love, Gilmore Girls offers seven seasons (and a four-part reunion series) of feel-good content. The young mom and her teenage daughter — played by Lauren Graham and Alexis Bledel, respectively — talk fast, drink a lot of coffee, and lean on each other through family drama, job changes, and romantic ups and downs. Hart of Dixie | HBO Max If you’re a fan of Gilmore Girls , this wholesome show will be right up your alley. Rachel Bilson stars as Zoe Hart, a doctor from New York City who inherits half of a family practice in the small, fictional town of Bluebell, Alabama: a perfectly cozy community where neighbors support each other, get tangled up in romance, and attend many a quirky festival. Home for Christmas | Netflix The first season of this Norwegian show follows Johanne, a 30-year-old single nurse, as she gives herself 24 days to find a boyfriend to bring home for Christmas. Three seasons later, the show (always set during the holidays) remains full of tender moments about navigating romance, independence, and family expectations. Is It Cake? | Netflix The premise is super simple and super silly: Contestants bake elaborate cakes that look like everyday items, including purses, paintings, and rubber ducks. The desserts are then placed next to the real objects they resemble, and guest judges have to guess which one is the cake. It’s fun to play along, though it’s delightfully tricky! Love on the Spectrum U.S. | Netflix There are plenty of reality shows about finding love, but Love on the Spectrum stands out — not only because its stars are neurodivergent but also because it possesses a warmth and hopefulness that make you truly root for the cast as they seek meaningful relationships. The U.S. version is a spinoff of the Australian series , and both are available to stream on Netflix. North of North | Netflix If you need a reminder that good things can come during uncertain times, this show fits the bill. Set in the tiny, fictional Arctic community of Ice Cove, North of North follows a young Inuk mother as she embarks on a new chapter after leaving her marriage. Viewers follow along with her highs and lows as she tries to get a handle on dating and building a career, while breaking down traditional gender expectations. Psych | Prime Video and Peacock Watch a quick-witted and perceptive police consultant (played by James Roday Rodriguez) solve cases using the power of observation — and the help of his reluctant BFF (played by Dulé Hill). The eight-season show combines comedy, drama, and detective work, all the while highlighting the infectious friendship between the two main characters. Tip: Keep an eye out for pineapples ! Queer Eye | Netflix The “Fab Five” gives emotional makeovers to ordinary folks across the country. But they don’t focus on appearance alone: The team explores the powerful connection between how we look, how we treat ourselves, and how we interact with the world — a reminder we can all use. Schitt’s Creek | Hulu Riches-to-rags is the premise of Schitt’s Creek : a series about a wealthy family who loses all their money and moves into a motel in a (very) small town. Laugh-out-loud moments, endearing friendships, and perfectly quotable one-liners earned this rewatchable, lighthearted show an Emmy for outstanding comedy in 2020. Shrinking | Apple TV On paper, Shrinking doesn’t sound particularly feel-good — it follows a father (played by Jason Segel) navigating parenthood and his career as a therapist following his wife’s sudden death. However, the show portrays grief through a lens that’s undeniably uplifting. It’s impossible not to fall in love with the nosy neighbors and hilarious coworkers, especially Paul, the lovably gruff mentor played by Harrison Ford (who earned his first Emmy nomination for the role at age 83). Sister, Sister | Paramount Plus A ’90s classic, Sister, Sister — starring twins Tia and Tamera Mowry — is still a joy to watch decades after it originally aired. Equally heart-filling and funny, the six-season series captures the magic of sisterhood and the positive impact of supportive family units. Somebody Feed Phil | Netflix There are many foodie travel shows out there, but this one has Phil Rosenthal. The creator of Everybody Loves Raymond supplies just the right amount of wholesome dad jokes as he tries local cuisine in Kyoto, Copenhagen, and Cape Town, among dozens of other cities around the world. All eight seasons are packed with enticing eats and conversations, but we’re partial to the first two, which include scenes of Rosenthal video chatting with his mom and dad before they passed away in 2019 and 2021, respectively. Somebody Somewhere | Prime Video Described as “a totally platonic love story” by HBO, Somebody Somewhere is about two coworkers (played by Bridget Everett and Jeff Hiller) who become dear friends. Audiences watch as they develop the sweetest bond that’s filled with lots of laughs and good vibes. “I hope that people come away with ‘never give up on yourself,’ because a lot of people do,” said Everett. St. Denis Medical | Peacock and Netflix Think of this as a hospital-centered version of The Office (another comfort TV favorite). This sitcom chronicles the day-to-day lives of nurses and surgeons as they navigate wacky medical scenarios and even wackier workplace dynamics. But we’d be remiss not to mention that there’s plenty of heart among the staff, who lean on each other as they care for patients. Stick | Apple TV A love letter to golf, Stick follows a former pro golfer seeking redemption by mentoring a teen prodigy who has his own complicated relationship with the game. The soun d track is stacked with hits, and you’ll never listen to “Cecilia” by Simon & Garfunkel the same way again. Survivor | Netflix (Select Seasons) and Paramount Plus (All Seasons) A show that just keeps on giving, Survivor has delivered over 50 seasons of real-life drama about “castaways” competing for a prize of $1 million. While the concept has remained mostly the same for more than two decades, every season delivers new personalities and social dynamics. Ted Lasso | Apple TV The epitome of comfort TV, Ted Lasso centers on an American football coach (Jason Sudeikis) who is hired to manage a British soccer team. Even if you’re not a sports fan, this four-season series is so charming and rich with wholesome humor that makes it a feel-good favorite for everyone. Tex Mex Motors | Netflix Watch old junkyard cars from Mexico get radically restored in Texas, thanks to a talented team of experts on Tex Mex Motors . While the car transformations are fun to watch (and very impressive), the restoration pros are the real stars of the show. The Dog House | HBO Max and Hulu ​If you haven’t watched The Dog House yet, you’re in for a treat. The unscripted show follows staff at a British animal rescue charity as they match pups with new pet parents. It’s a joy watching people light up when they fall in love with their new best friend — and of course, seeing the pups fall in love with their new best friends, too. The Durrells in Corfu | PBS and Prime Video The Durrells in Corfu is a British series based on memoirs about a family who left England for Greece in the 1930s. Not only is the story full of wit and heart, but it’s also set in the dreamiest of settings. And after you watch the show’s four seasons, we recommend checking out this documentary about the real Durrells . The Great British Baking Show | Netflix Of all the comfort shows streaming lately, The Great British Baking Show (titled The Great British Bake Off in the U.K.) takes the cake — pun intended. Each week, contestants bake all kinds of mouthwatering treats in hopes of making it to the finale, where one talented baker earns the coveted cake stand and is crowned winner. But unlike so many other competition shows that can feel cutthroat, the judges offer kind, constructive feedback, and the contestants often help one another finish their creations. You can stream most seasons on Netflix, including the most recent with new judge Nigella Lawson, a star addition as far as the Nice News team is concerned. Younger | Netflix In Younger , Liza, a 40-year-old mom (played by Sutton Foster), pretends to be in her 20s to land an entry-level assistant job at a publishing house in New York alongside Kelsey (played by Hilary Duff). A love triangle, book deals, and many stories of female friendship ensue over seven seasons of lighthearted TV. Highly recommend for fans of Lizzie McGuire .
