items.description: Το 2019, μια οικογένεια στο Λος Άντζελες ετοιμαζόταν να μετακομίσει στο Σαν Ντιέγκο όταν το κόκερ σπάνιελ τους, το Corduroy, εξαφανίστηκε. «Η εξαφάνισή του ράγισε τις καρδιές τους, ειδικά τον καλύτερο φίλο του, τη μικρή κόρη της Samantha», έγραψε η Los Angeles Animal Services σε μια ανάρτηση στα μέσα κοινωνικής δικτύωσης. Μετακόμισαν χωρίς αυτόν και πέρασαν επτά χρόνια. Μετά, τον Οκτώβριο, ένα παλιό…
items.descriptionOriginal: In 2019, a family in Los Angeles was getting ready to move to San Diego when their cocker spaniel, Corduroy, went missing . “His disappearance broke their hearts, especially his best friend, Samantha’s young daughter,” Los Angeles Animal Services wrote in a social media post. They moved without him, and seven years passed. Then, in October, an older cocker spaniel came into LA Animal Services’ North Central Shelter . Nobody knows where Corduroy had been for all that time, but his microchip still led straight to his family, who were still living in San Diego. They drove up to get him. “They made the trip from San Diego to bring him home, and the reunion was filled with hugs, smiles, and happy tears,” the shelter wrote, according to KTLA . LA Animal Services shared two photos side by side: Samantha’s daughter as a little girl, hugging Corduroy on the steps, and the two of them together again seven years later. “Corduroy’s story is a powerful reminder: microchips help bring lost pets home, even years later!” the shelter added. It’s important to note that the chip only worked because the family’s contact information on it was still current. A microchip is just an ID number; if the phone number registered to it is no longer active, the scan leads nowhere. All six LA Animal Services shelters offer microchipping. View this post on Instagram The post A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: What if a recipe passed down through generations could become a ₹75 crore business? ❤️ At just 20, Veena Devi began earning to support her family. From stitching cloth bags and selling sattu to teaching Hindi for 12 years, she worked hard to educate her children. Little did she know that a recipe she learnt from her mother-in-law would one day change her life. What started with homemade thekua, gujiya and namkeen for her daughter’s birthday grew into MomsMade, a homegrown snacks brand now reaching over 3 lakh households across India. From a small kitchen in Bengaluru, Veena built a business dispatching 1,200–1,500 orders every day and earning around ₹2.5 crore in monthly revenue. Today, her children are helping take the dream forward. From Gopalganj, Bihar, to homes across India, Veena is doing more than building a business, she is keeping generations of homemade food traditions alive. #MomsMade #WomenEntrepreneurs #BiharEntrepreneur #Thekua #BihariFood #IndianEntrepreneurs #WomenInBusiness #HomemadeSnacks #BusinessSuccessStory #SmallBusinessIndia #BiharPride #FoodBusiness #TheBetterIndia

items.descriptionOriginal: "Six months ago, on the other side of the road, my life was something I wanted to come out of. Now, I have crossed the road, and everything is going well." On a busy road in Bengaluru's Koramangala, Parthiban sometimes looks at the BDO (Binder Dijker Otte) office differently. Today, he walks through its doors as an Article Assistant, one step closer to becoming a chartered accountant. But before joining BDO in April 2026, he knew the building from across the road. On one side was the Zepto store where he packed orders and the PG where he lived. On the other was the brightly lit BDO office. During tea breaks, he would look at it and wonder if he could one day work there. "I have crossed the road," he says. "Whenever I feel work pressure now, I think about the past. I have dreamt a lot and struggled a lot to reach this. " The road to that office involved failed CA Intermediate attempts, financial uncertainty, a close friend's bereavement, exhausting shifts at a warehouse, bicycle deliveries across Bengaluru and studying whenever he could find a few minutes. But Parthiban kept going. The dream that survived two failures Parthiban grew up in Kanchipuram, Tamil Nadu, in a family where resources were limited but his ambitions were encouraged. His father is a Nadaswaram player who studied until Class 3, while his mother, K Mahalakshmi, is a homemaker who studied until Class 12. As the first-generation graduate in the family, Parthiban knew that becoming a professional would mean a lot to his parents. Parthiban's journey from a delivery executive in Bengaluru to a CA Finalist was shaped by persistence, hard work and a determination to keep studying. His CA journey began with a decision he made during the COVID-19 period. In Class 9, unsure about what he wanted to pursue, he spent three days researching careers on his phone, from medicine and engineering to commerce. Eventually, he chose CA. He took science in Classes 11 and 12 on his mother's advice so he could keep his options open. After Class 12, he moved to Chennai and joined coaching for CA Foundation. The first step went remarkably well. Parthiban cleared Foundation in his first attempt with 305 out of 400, earning a distinction. His preparation was simple but consistent: attend classes, revise every day and take weekly tests. When accounts felt unfamiliar among students from a commerce background, he turned to YouTube. For some concepts, he watched five or six different videos until the basics became clear. CA Intermediate, however, proved much harder. The syllabus was larger, and the routine that had worked for Foundation became difficult to maintain. He failed his first attempt. The result affected his confidence deeply. "I lost myself actually," he says. "I faced many inferiority complexes, and that affected my preparation." Three months later, he attempted the exam again. He failed again. For his mother, those results were painful to watch. "His first CA Intermediate failure affected him deeply. He was completely heartbroken and emotionally shattered after seeing the result," she says. "Each time he checked the results portal and saw an unsuccessful outcome, it affected him greatly." Yet he never wanted to quit. "He never wanted to quit CA because it was a course he had chosen for himself," Mahalakshmi says. "However, after every unsuccessful attempt, he felt guilty about asking us to support him for the next exam ." By September 2025, circumstances at home also forced Parthiban to make another difficult decision. After giving his third attempt on 15 September, he travelled alone to Bengaluru the next day. He had one plan: find work, support himself and continue studying. Studying between shifts and deliveries Parthiban initially wanted to work as a delivery executive but could not find an electric vehicle. After two days of searching across areas such as JP Nagar and Jayanagar, he found work through a vendor at a Zepto store in Koramangala. His shift was officially 5 pm to 2 am. During busy periods, it stretched to 3 or 4 am, and sometimes even until 7 am. As an order packer, he spent six to seven hours running around the store, collecting and packing orders. The warehouse had several temperature-controlled zones. The freezer room was around 0 C, while the ice zone, where ice creams were stored, could be as cold as minus 15 C to minus 20 C. Late-night ice cream orders meant he sometimes had to search the freezing room around midnight. "After only two minutes, our nails become red and then it feels like something senseless," he recalls. Between late-night warehouse shifts and bicycle deliveries, Parthiban found small pockets of time to prepare for his CA Intermediate examinations. Even meals had to fit around the work. His PG was nearby, so when he got a few minutes, he would rush back, eat and return. For the first 15 days, he managed to study during the day and work at night. Then came another blow. A close friend he had met during CA Foundation lost her mother. Parthiban wanted to be with her and her family, but Zepto's strict working hours made it difficult to take leave. After working through the Diwali peak period, he resigned. He took a five-day break and then started working as a Blinkit bicycle delivery partner. He rented a cycle for Rs 600 a month because he did not want to depend on his parents financially. The work was physically demanding. On weekends, when incentives were higher, he sometimes rode 90 to 100 km in a day, working from the morning and returning to deliveries in the evening until 11 pm, midnight or even 1 am. But he carried his CA preparation into those hours too. Because Blinkit sometimes gave him only two or three orders an hour, he could get 20-minute gaps between deliveries. He used those breaks to watch marathon CA lectures on YouTube. Then, on 3 November 2025, the September exam results arrived and Parthiban had cleared one group of CA Intermediate. He continued working, however, because there was another attempt ahead. Then came an incident that made him rethink how he was spending those remaining weeks. One Sunday, after riding for hours, he was given a five-kilometre transfer order by another delivery executive. Already exhausted, Parthiban asked customer support and the store to cancel or reassign it. Instead, he was told that refusing could result in his ID being blocked. He called the customer. The first time, the call was cut. The second time, it happened again. On the third call, Parthiban says he literally begged the customer to listen. The customer told him he had one minute to explain and began counting. "1, 2, 3, 4…" The call was cut again. Five minutes later, the customer cancelled the order himself. "I was helpless," Parthiban recalls. "I was very much disturbed that day." That experience, combined with the limited time before his next attempt, pushed him to make a choice: go home and give the exam his full attention. Back home, he changed how he studied Back home, Parthiban had more than 45 days to prepare. This time, he did not simply study harder. He studied differently. After two unsuccessful attempts and a third in which he cleared one group, he went back to his mistakes and identified what needed to change. He divided his preparation into blocks of around 15 to 20 days per subject. He also changed his exam strategy. After two unsuccessful attempts at CA Intermediate, Parthiban reworked his study strategy and continued working towards his dream. In the tax paper, for example, he decided to attempt the smaller questions and MCQs first before moving to the compulsory question. The goal was to manage his time better and reach the 150 marks he needed. "I pointed out all the mistakes I had made in that attempt," he says. "I made some small changes, and that really helped me." The success of clearing one group had also given him confidence. Through it all, his parents continued to support him. "We never blamed or criticised him because we knew it could affect him emotionally, " says Mahalakshmi. "We understood the difficulty of the course, encouraged him to stay positive and reassured him that setbacks are a part of the learning process." After clearing both groups of CA Intermediate, Parthiban joined BDO's Bengaluru office as an Article Assistant on 2 April 2026. His sisters, Anuja and Supraja, were another important source of emotional support. Parthiban says they were people he could talk to during his difficult phases when he found it hard to share everything with his parents. Then, on 8 March 2026, came the result he had been working towards. He cleared the second group of CA Intermediate. Parthiban was now a CA Finalist. Six months later, he was on the other side The happiness at home was immense. "We were extremely happy and proud when he cleared CA Intermediate," Mahalakshmi says. "It felt like all his hard work, sacrifices and perseverance had finally paid off." A week later, Parthiban interviewed at four firms. He was selected by three. Parthiban joined BDO's Bengaluru office in April 2026, the same workplace he had once looked at from across the road during his tea breaks. One of them was BDO. He joined the Bengaluru office as an Article Assistant on 2 April 2026. The full-circle moment was not lost on him. Six months earlier, he had been working across the road. Now, he was walking into the very office he had once looked at during his tea breaks. His colleague Dharshan KS, a Senior Article at BDO, says Parthiban's determination was evident from the beginning. "He never lets circumstances limit his ambitions," Dharshan says. "His work ethic, humility and commitment to continuous learning stood out from day one." What also stood out was his kindness. "He connects easily with people from all backgrounds, is approachable, and helps create a positive and comfortable environment within the team." For Parthiban, being treated with respect had taken on particular meaning during his months in delivery work. During his time as a delivery executive, Parthiban was often treated differently because of the job he was doing. He recalls being scolded by motorists and encountering customers who treated him with suspicion. he office he once hoped to work in became his workplace when Parthiban joined BDO as an Article Assistant. At Zepto too, he experienced people using harsh words with him. He does not believe people need to be treated differently because of their education, profession or position. "Respect should be given to everyone," he says. "It should not be selective. Every person deserves some respect." What he wants other CA aspirants to know Parthiban is still an Article Assistant, with his CA Final examinations ahead. But the young man who once struggled with repeated failure now looks at setbacks differently. He calls his journey a "survival journey", one that taught him lessons far beyond his textbooks. His message to CA aspirants facing failure is simple. "Failures are common in CA," he says. "Even though we know that, whenever we see that result on the screen, it really affects us." But failure also taught him how precious success can feel. He explains it through food: the same meal may seem ordinary to someone who eats three times a day, but to someone who has gone without food for a week, it becomes something precious. For Parthiban, the road across from the Zepto store to the BDO office represents six months of hard work, difficult choices and a dream that stayed alive. "Once you face failure, you can experience the taste of success fully," he says. For Parthiban, that taste came after years of studying, failing, working, cycling through Bengaluru and finding lessons in places he never expected. And when work becomes difficult at BDO, he remembers the Zepto store across the road and the tea breaks when he wondered if he might one day work in the very office where he now sits. All images courtesy of CA Parthiban

items.descriptionOriginal: In the last couple of decades, many companies have reduced the heft of plastic bottles , cardboard boxes, paper envelopes, and other packaging materials, a strategy known as lightweighting. At first glance, this seems like a win-win: less material means lower costs and a lighter burden on the environment. But the approach may also backfire, a new study suggests. Researchers found that people are more likely to throw lightweight packaging away, and less likely to recycle it, compared to more substantial packaging materials. “Even well-intended sustainability practices can have unexpected negative consequences,” the researchers write. First, the researchers set out to determine the scope of the problem. A small pilot study at a university campus event and a larger week-long audit of trash and recycling bins on campus showed that lighter-weight recyclable plastic beverage containers were more likely to end up in the trash compared to more substantial plastic cups and bottles. “Once low-density packaging gets into consumers’ hands, it produces more waste, as consumers are more likely to improperly trash low-density versus high-density recyclable packaging,” the researchers write. Investigating causal relationships, the researchers concocted a laboratory study in which participants were asked to assess the properties of a piece of paper—either flimsy newsprint or sturdy cardstock—which they were instructed to dispose of at the end of the experiment. As expected, participants rated the thinner paper as lower quality than the thicker paper and were more likely to throw it in the trash at the end of the experiment—although a statistical analysis people get from recycling has a downside More details about the nuances of people’s thought processes emerged from an online experiment in which participants imagined receiving a takeout meal in either a thin paper bakery bag or a thick paper grocery bag. “Where would you put this bag?” they were asked. The participants then rated the quality of the bag, assessed its value, and indicated their level of discomfort about putting the bag in the garbage. “Ultimately, we find that consumers are more apt to throw low-density packaging in the trash because it is perceived as being more disposable (i.e., lower in value and associated with lesser feelings of waste aversion),” the researchers write. So far, so hopeless, given the human foibles and imperfect decision-making. But the solution could be a relatively simple one, according to the new work. In both an online study and a small field trial, the researchers found evidence that including a message on lightweight packaging—for example, “You may be done with this envelope, but it still has value”—increased the likelihood that the material would make it to the recycling bin. “Prompting consumers to reconsider the value of low-density packaging can curtail this unintended wastefulness,” the researchers write. Issuing such prompts is in companies’ own best interests, the researchers point out. In addition to lightweighting, many firms aim to increase the proportion of recycled material in their packaging. And where is that recycled material going to come from if consumers have thrown the previous iteration of that packaging in the trash? Source: Loomer L. and S.C. Whitley . “ Through thick and thin? When sustainable package design increases consumer waste generation .” Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science 2026. Image: © Anthropocene Magazine.

items.descriptionOriginal: For a village that depends on the monsoon, a pond can make the difference between rainwater that runs away and water that remains available after the rains. It can collect rainfall, support nearby farms and, depending on the soil and water conditions, help replenish groundwater. Over time, however, silt, waste and neglect can reduce how much water a pond holds. In Haryana's Rewari district, where groundwater has been under pressure for years, 10 village ponds are now at the centre of a new conservation effort. The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) and Nokia India have joined hands to restore these waterbodies over 24 months, with a target of increasing their combined storage capacity to 120 million litres. The project, announced on 10 November 2026, also plans to plant native vegetation, improve public spaces around the ponds and involve villagers in their upkeep. If the work achieves its goals, around 22,000 people could benefit directly, while another 50,000 could benefit indirectly. Why Rewari is turning back to its ponds Rewari's water worries are not new. In 2019, a Government of India report under the Jal Shakti Abhiyan described the district as water-stressed. It said groundwater levels had been declining, with conditions especially serious in Khol block, classified as over-exploited. That means water was being drawn from underground faster than it could be naturally replenished. For communities that rely on groundwater for everyday needs and farming, this makes conserving every possible source of water important. At the time, the district administration had begun mapping existing water resources. Gram Panchayats made inventories of village ponds and other water structures, helping officials identify what could be repaired or improved. Residents, farmers and Gram Panchayats can also help monitor water levels, identify pollution sources and report maintenance requirements. Photograph: (Deepanwita Gita Niyogi for 101Reporters) The idea was to make better use of the systems that villages already had. Traditional ponds are part of that picture. When cared for, they can hold rainwater, provide habitat for small wildlife and help water soak into the ground where conditions permit. When their inlets get blocked or their storage space fills with sediment, they become less effective. The new Rewari project builds on the wider need to protect these familiar but valuable waterbodies. What will change around the 10 ponds? TERI and Nokia India signed a memorandum of understanding at TERI Gram in Gwal Pahari, Haryana, to begin the Nokia Pond Rejuvenation Project. The plan is to enhance the ponds' combined water storage capacity to 1,20,000 cubic metres, or 120 million litres. This is a target for the coming two years, rather than water already conserved. For villagers, the potential value is straightforward: ponds that can collect and retain more water may help support local water needs and contribute to groundwater recharge. The project also aims to improve the land around the ponds through native planting. Plants suited to the area can help hold pond banks together, slow rainwater runoff and trap some of the soil that might otherwise wash into the water. A 2022 review published in the journal Wetlands explains that vegetated areas around ponds can reduce sediment and pollutants entering them, while supporting the surrounding ecosystem. But planting alone is not enough. The choice of species, where they are placed and whether they survive will shape their usefulness. TERI's announcement includes native planting , although the number of individual plants and the species to be used still need clarification. Alongside the ecological work, the initiative proposes 100 streetlights, benches and dustbins around the ponds. These additions are intended to make the spaces safer and easier for residents to use and care for. Who will look after the ponds afterwards? A restored pond can deteriorate again if rubbish collects, channels become blocked or new plants are left without care. That is why the project includes community participation rather than treating restoration as a one-time construction job. Residents and Gram Panchayats could help identify problems, discourage dumping and raise maintenance concerns . Farmers, too, have a stake in protecting water sources that may support agriculture. At the project announcement, Dr Dipankar Saharia, Executive Director of TERI, spoke about "community-led conservation" and securing water for communities and farms. The involvement of local people will matter particularly after the 24-month project ends. The ponds will need attention through changing seasons, including when there is little rainfall. 🤝 TERI and Nokia India Join Hands to Strengthen Water Security in Haryana TERI and Nokia India recently signed an MoU to launch a pond rejuvenation initiative in Rewari, Haryana, aimed at improving local water security through ecological restoration and community participation. The MoU was signed by Dr Dipankar Saharia, Executive Director, TERI, and Ms Vibha Mehra, India Country Manager, Nokia, at TERI Gram, Gwal Pahari. The programme seeks to address water stress in one of India's key agricultural and industrial regions while supporting sustainable natural resource management. Supported under Nokia India's CSR programme, the initiative will focus on the rejuvenation of approximately 10 ponds, alongside native tree plantation and community engagement activities designed to promote long-term environmental stewardship. The partnership reflects a shared commitment to creating meaningful impact through community-led environmental action and advancing India's sustainable development goals. @sahariadipankar | @nokia | #WaterSecurity #PondRejuvenation #CSR #Sustainability #ClimateAction #CommunityDevelopment #EnvironmentalStewardship — TERI (@teriin) November 10, 2026 TERI estimates that 22,000 people could benefit directly and a further 50,000 indirectly, based on Census 2011 figures. Those are projected benefits, and the actual results will depend on the restoration work and long-term maintenance . The real test will be whether water continues to reach the ponds, their banks remain protected and residents have support to maintain them. For Rewari, the promise of the initiative is rooted in something villages have known for generations: a pond is useful when it holds water and people continue to care for it. If these 10 ponds become healthier and remain that way, their value could be felt in the everyday lives of the communities around them, long after the last bench is installed and the restoration teams have left. Sources: 'TERI and Nokia India Sign MoU to Rejuvenate 10 Ponds in Haryana's Rewari District' : Published on 10 November 2026 'Rewari outlines district water conservation plan' : By Ministry of Water Resources, Published on 25 November 2019 'Current Status of Ponds in India: A Framework for Restoration, Policies and Circular Economy' : By Shweta Yadav, V.C Goyal, Published on 4 November 2022

Η πρόσβαση στη σωστή φροντίδα μπορεί να αλλάξει αυτό το ταξίδι - από την έγκαιρη εύρεση του καρκίνου και την υποστήριξη της θεραπείας έως τη βοήθεια των ασθενών να ζουν με αξιοπρέπεια όταν η θεραπεία δεν είναι πλέον για θεραπεία. Μέσω της συνεργασίας της με ιδρύματα υγείας…
items.descriptionOriginal: Cancer changes more than the person diagnosed. It can disrupt work, finances, families, and the everyday life around them. Access to the right care can change that journey - from finding cancer early and supporting treatment to helping patients live with dignity when treatment is no longer about a cure. Through its work with healthcare institutions and communities, Alkem Foundation is working to make quality cancer care more accessible and more complete. Από τους αξέχαστους τερματισμούς του τελευταίου έως τους πέντε τίτλους IPL, ο MS Dhoni χάρισε στους θαυμαστές του Chennai Super Kings αναμνήσεις που θα αγαπούν για πάντα. items.descriptionOriginal: For 18 seasons, one man made millions believe that no match was over until he said so. From unforgettable last-over finishes to five IPL titles, MS Dhoni gave Chennai Super Kings fans memories they will cherish forever. When Dhoni became the first player to captain CSK in 200 IPL matches in 2023, Sunil Gavaskar said there would never be another captain like him. Today, as Dhoni announces his retirement as an IPL player, those words hit differently. The captain may be stepping away from the field, but his bond with CSK continues as he takes on the role of Team Mentor. Thank you for the memories, Thala! 💛 What’s your most unforgettable Dhoni moment? #MSDhoni #Thala #ChennaiSuperKings #CSK #ForOurThala [MS Dhoni retirement from IPL, MS Dhoni CSK Team Mentor, MS Dhoni retirement news, Chennai Super Kings, Thala Dhoni legacy]

items.descriptionOriginal: Every winter, the burning of leftover paddy stubble across northern India adds to seasonal air pollution, particularly in the Indo-Gangetic plains. For farmers working against tight turnaround times between harvesting one crop and sowing the next, clearing agricultural residue quickly and affordably remains a challenge. Takachar, an Indian climate-tech startup co-founded by Vidyut Mohan and Kevin Kung, is working to address this problem with portable technology that converts crop residue into biochar and other useful products instead of allowing it to go up in smoke. The innovation received international recognition when it won the Clean Our Air category at the 2021 Earthshot Prize. With the 2026 edition of the global environmental award set to announce its winners in Mumbai on 17 November, Takachar's work offers an example of how technology can connect agricultural waste management with cleaner air and potential income opportunities for farmers. The Better India previously featured the startup's work in February this year, documenting how farmers in Punjab were using its technology to turn agricultural stubble into biochar. Turning agricultural waste into a resource For farmers, disposing of crop residue after harvesting can be both time-consuming and expensive. Paddy stubble is bulky, and transporting it to processing facilities adds to operational costs. Burning it in fields is often a quicker option, despite its environmental consequences. Takachar aims to make processing easier by taking the equipment closer to where agricultural residue is generated. The startup has developed a portable, tractor-mounted thermochemical device that heats crop residue at temperatures ranging from 400 to 700 degrees Celsius in a low-oxygen environment. This process converts the biomass into carbon-rich biochar. Unlike conventional open-field burning, which releases pollutants into the atmosphere, the technology processes agricultural residue into a material that can be put to further use. Each unit can process up to one metric tonne of stubble per hour, making it suitable for village-level operations. The resulting biochar can be applied to agricultural soil to improve soil health or sold for use as biofuel. Making stubble management more accessible One of the biggest challenges in addressing stubble burning is ensuring that alternatives are both accessible and economically viable for farmers, particularly those with limited resources. By making its equipment portable and tractor-compatible, Takachar aims to reduce the logistical difficulties associated with transporting bulky agricultural residue over long distances. The approach also creates opportunities to turn what was once considered agricultural waste into a useful product. Farmers can use the resulting biochar on their own land or explore markets for surplus material. The innovation received international recognition when it won the Clean Our Air category at the 2021 Earthshot Prize. Photograph: ( The Global Indian ; harmonious entrepreneurship ) The Better India's February coverage also reported a nearly 90% reduction in stubble burning in Punjab over a single season. From a 2021 Earthshot win to wider recognition When Takachar won the Clean Our Air category at the 2021 Earthshot Prize, the start up received 1 million that helped the team accelerate product prototyping, expand its workforce and increase investment in research and development. The funding also supported the development and commercialisation of its Takavator Mini unit , which can process up to 100 kilograms of biomass input per hour. The organisation reports that the technology has since been deployed in multiple locations around the world. The 2026 Earthshot Prize finalists were announced on 18 September, with 15 solutions selected across five environmental categories. The winners will be announced at the awards ceremony in Mumbai on 17 November, with five solutions set to receive 1 million each to scale their work. As India continues to address the recurring challenge of agricultural residue burning , Takachar's work demonstrates how decentralised technology can connect waste processing, farmer livelihoods and air pollution reduction. Its approach centres on a simple but important question: can the residue left behind after a harvest become a resource that farmers have a reason to collect and use, rather than burn? Sources: Earthshot Prize 2026

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Geography, Not Technology, Holds Back Reusing Retired EV Batteries for Climate Gains Reading Time: 3 minutes Moving old batteries between Chinese provinces could unlock 6 billion tons of emissions savings by 2050, a key to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains, according to a study. Reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains begins with a simple fact. An electric vehicle (EV) battery usually leaves the car when its capacity drops to about 80%. That leftover capacity can still store solar and wind power for years. In China, the problem is location. Most batteries retire in wealthy eastern provinces, where EV ownership is highest. The wind and solar farms that need storage sit mainly in the west. Much of the batteries’ value is already slipping away. In 2022 alone, about 465,000 tons of retired batteries in China went to waste locally. Researchers at Fudan University in Shanghai have now measured the cost of this mismatch. Their August 2026 study finds it strands about 6 billion tons of carbon savings through 2050. That is roughly a full year of US greenhouse gas emissions. The team published its findings in Environmental Science and Ecotechnology. Its province-by-province model tracks where batteries retire, where they could be reused, and what each option costs. China, the world’s largest EV market, offers a critical test case. Retired batteries can take three main paths. Metallurgical recycling, the most common route, breaks batteries down to recover metals. Direct recycling restores battery materials without breaking down their chemical structure. This keeps more of the value built into the original battery. Storage reuse gives whole batteries a second job. Those last two options deliver far more value. Scenarios that favor storage or direct recycling produced three to five times the cost savings of metallurgical recycling. They also cut emissions by one to three times as much. The study maps the storage mismatch in detail. By 2050, Inner Mongolia alone could be short about 340 gigawatt-hours of storage batteries. Meanwhile, Guangdong and Shandong could each have surpluses of more than 220 gigawatt-hours. Direct recycling needs batteries in manufacturing regions with specialized factories. Under that scenario, Guangdong and Fujian each face shortfalls of thousands of gigawatt-hours. Other provinces would hold surpluses. The gap will widen as eastern EV sales rise and western wind and solar farms expand. In a storage-focused scenario, a 0-to-1 measure of regional imbalance rises from 0.6 in 2035 to 0.7 in 2050. Left alone, this mismatch undercuts the climate gains of reusing retired EV batteries. Without moving batteries between provinces, 50 to 87% of the possible cost savings disappear. Up to 53% of the possible emissions cuts are lost as well. Moving the batteries is cheap by comparison. In the direct recycling scenario, transporting every 100 yuan saved would cost only about 2.3 yuan. Transport emissions would offset just 0.01 to 0.03% of the climate gains. A Fudan University study finds that moving batteries between provinces is central to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains in China. Photo by Nico Kusuma Jaya on Pexels. Safe handling is essential to reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains. Retired batteries can leak, deform, or catch fire in transit, and they cannot be stacked like ordinary freight. Specialized transport vehicles exist but remain scarce in China. Paperwork adds another hurdle. Because retired batteries count as hazardous materials, both the sending and receiving provinces must approve each transfer. The researchers call for a streamlined national transport network to cut these delays. Those barriers have side effects. Limited transport and processing capacity pushes many batteries into illegal channels. The authors urge stronger penalties for unlicensed recyclers and subsidies for proper disposal. The study’s best scenario gradually shifts away from metallurgical recycling after 2030. By 2050, direct recycling would handle about 56% of collected batteries, and storage would handle about 24%. It would save about 6.1 billion tons of emissions and nearly 4 trillion yuan, about USD 550 billion. Reuse and recycling work together in this plan. Batteries used for storage typically return to recycling within about six years, once capacity falls to 40 to 50%. Each battery can serve cars, then the power grid, and then supply materials for new batteries. The researchers argue that planning, not technology, is the main barrier. Early, coordinated investment in transport and treatment sites could turn spatial barriers into climate and economic gains. Waiting risks locking companies into lower-value metallurgical recycling. China is not alone in this challenge. Europe and the United States face similar splits between where people drive EVs and where renewable power is produced. The authors suggest their model could support reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains there too. The findings come from modeling, so real results will depend on investment, safety rules, and market demand. Building treatment capacity in the right places will also take time. As EV adoption grows, the number of retiring batteries will only rise. Reusing retired EV batteries for climate gains will depend less on new inventions than on trucks, permits, and planning. Getting old batteries to the right place may be one of the simplest climate wins available. The post Geography, Not Technology, Holds Back Reusing Retired EV Batteries for Climate Gains appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: If you stepped outside in Gurugram on Sunday, November 15, the change in the air may have felt noticeable. After days of hazy skies and pollution-heavy mornings, light showers brought a brief spell of relief. The rain, accompanied by stronger surface winds, appeared to clear some of the suspended dust and improve visibility across parts of Delhi-NCR. The change was reflected in the numbers, too. According to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Gurugram's average Air Quality Index (AQI) dropped from 340 on Saturday, November 14, to 283 on Sunday, moving from the 'very poor' to the 'poor' category. This came after six consecutive days of very poor air quality. For residents who had been waking up to hazy skies, the showers offered a welcome break. But there is a catch: cleaner-looking skies do not necessarily mean clean air. So, does rain really wash pollution away? And if it does, why does the relief often disappear within a day or two? How rain acts as nature's air purifier There is some science behind that fresh-after-rain feeling. When raindrops fall through the atmosphere, they collide with suspended dust, smoke and other airborne particles, collecting some of them and carrying them down to the ground. Scientists call this process wet deposition , commonly referred to as atmospheric washout. Think of it as nature's way of rinsing the air. As droplets travel downwards, they capture pollutants through processes such as interception and impaction. These particles then settle on roads, rooftops, trees and other surfaces along with the rainwater. However, rain does not remove every pollutant equally well. Rain can wash some suspended dust and pollutants out of the atmosphere, offering temporary relief from poor air quality. Photograph: ( DD India ) Larger particles, such as PM10 (particulate matter measuring up to 10 micrometres), are generally easier for raindrops to capture. Fine particles, particularly PM2.5 (measuring 2.5 micrometres or smaller), are much harder to remove efficiently. This distinction matters because PM2.5 can penetrate deep into the lungs and is a major concern during Delhi-NCR's winter pollution episodes. The intensity and duration of rainfall also matter. A sustained spell of rain generally has more opportunity to wash particles out of the atmosphere than a brief drizzle. A few passing showers may clear some dust without making a significant difference to the finer pollution particles. Why the wind matters as much as the rain In Gurugram, the November 15 improvement was not simply a result of rainfall. Stronger surface winds played an important role, too. Rain helps remove pollutants from the atmosphere , while wind helps disperse them. When winds move at higher speeds, they can carry polluted air away and bring in relatively cleaner air from surrounding areas. This is particularly important during winter, when Delhi-NCR experiences conditions that allow pollution to accumulate close to the ground. The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) explains that low wind speeds, a shallow atmospheric mixing layer, and stagnant weather conditions restrict the dispersal of pollutants. In simple terms, there is less vertical and horizontal movement to spread pollution out. Fine particulate matter such as PM2.5 is harder to remove through rainfall and can continue to pose health risks even after the skies clear. Photograph: ( India Today ) When stronger winds arrive, they can break this stagnation, allowing pollutants to disperse. This means that a combination of rainfall and favourable wind conditions can produce a more noticeable improvement than either weather event alone. Why does the pollution return after the rain? If rain can wash away airborne particles, why does the AQI climb again so quickly? The answer lies in the fact that rainfall removes some of the pollution already present in the air, but it does not switch off the sources producing it. Vehicles continue to release exhaust, construction activity generates dust, industries emit pollutants, and biomass burning contributes to particulate matter. Once the rain stops and the atmosphere becomes stagnant again, these emissions can accumulate. Winter conditions make this worse. Lower temperatures and reduced atmospheric mixing can trap pollutants near the surface, allowing concentrations to rise again. There is another complication: high humidity can cause certain airborne particles to absorb moisture and grow in size. This can affect how they scatter light, making the atmosphere look hazier even when the underlying pollutant concentrations have not changed in the same way. A clearer sky is not always cleaner air The next time it rains after a particularly polluted spell, it is worth remembering that a blue patch of sky is not an air-quality certificate. The AQI is calculated using measured concentrations of pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide and ozone. Visibility, on the other hand, is influenced by several factors, including humidity, fog and suspended particles. Stronger surface winds help disperse accumulated pollutants, making them an important factor in improving Delhi-NCR's winter air quality. Photograph: ( AQI.in ) The rain may have made stepping outside a little more pleasant that Sunday, but Gurugram's AQI was a reminder that the relief would not last on its own. Once the showers stopped, the familiar sources of pollution were still there: vehicles on the roads, dust from construction sites and emissions from surrounding areas. And that is perhaps the most important distinction: rain can give us a temporary break from polluted air, but cleaner air is something we have to work towards long after the clouds have passed. Sources: 'Gurugram's AQI improves to 'poor' after six consecutive days of 'very poor' air' by Vidhi Bhutra for Hindustan Times, Published on 16 November 2026. 'What Rain Really Does to Air Quality: Myths vs Facts' by Equinox Labs, Published on 29 September 2026. 'Does Rain Improve Air Quality? What You Should Know' by IAQ Answers, Published on 28 September 2026.

items.descriptionOriginal: W hat might it be like to be a bird? Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles. “Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough grassland in which to hunt voles and mice, and space undisturbed by people and dogs. Suddenly the landscape around Lawy looked more like a series of obstacles and threats a wild animal needed to conquer: “Once I really began to delve into what it might be like to be a kestrel, I realized actually my options were very limited because it’s so difficult to find areas where I can find food.” Clatworthy dam impounds the headwaters of the River Tone. © River Tone Lawy’s experience is part of a pioneering experiment by Accelerator for Systemic Risk Assessment (ASRA), an independent nonprofit initiative hosted by the United Nations Foundation in collaboration with the University of the West of England (UWE) and funded by the Ecological Citizen(s) Network . The project, Risks Beyond Human Eyes, asks people around the River Tone catchment to explore risks not from the conventional perspective of human visitors, landowners, planners or conservationists, but through the sensory worlds and needs of other species: fierce otter, threatened salmon, quiet red deer, sharp-sighted kestrel or blind earthworm. Over a period of several months, 18 participants swam like salmon, surfed the river to mimic how an otter might glide through the water, or hid in hollows like earthworms. The setup sounds fanciful until its practical implications emerge: If conventional risk assessments systematically overlook what matters to other species, could temporarily shifting the human viewpoint reveal problems — and solutions — that would otherwise remain invisible? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] For Lawy, it has already changed how she manages land. She came to the project as a local resident, concerned about the water quality of the River Tone. People want to bathe in it, yet the water is too polluted with runoff from the nearby fields, herbicides, pesticides and other toxins. “But animals haven’t got that choice,” she says. “They are constantly living in this very poor-quality water.” These insights are part of the logic of the ASRA project, challenging the human-centeredness of conventional risk assessment. “Of course we’re not pretending that a person literally becomes an otter or kestrel,” project co-director Phil Tovey explains, “but this kind of disciplined attention exposes aspects of an animal’s environment that humans routinely fail to notice.” The resulting testimonies are not intended simply to produce moving stories about wildlife, but are treated as input to a wider systemic-risk assessment, alongside scientific and other evidence such as water quality. Participants in the project working on a course of action. Credit: Darren Honeywell According to the 2026 Living Planet Index , freshwater species populations declined by 85 percent between 1970 and 2022 , the steepest decline of any of the major ecosystems assessed. It’s one thing to read this number as an intellectual piece of information and another to attempt the perspective of a salmon, like some of the study participants, and arrive at the life-threatening realization that they couldn’t overcome a river barrier to get to their food source. Lawy experienced firsthand that a landscape designed to look accessible and attractive to humans appears radically different to a species trying to feed and reproduce. While repeatedly sitting outside over several weeks, Lawy never actually saw a kestrel. There were too many people, too many dogs, too much disturbance. “Kestrels actually need some space from us,” she realized. Lawy also saw the hay meadows in a different light. Once the hay is cut, Lawy suddenly noticed, the landscape can become a stark, hostile expanse. “There is no cover,” she says. During a hot, dry summer, that lack of shelter can mean the difference between life and death. At the next meeting of Friends of Longrun Meadow, Lawy proposed a “mosaic of habitats,” retaining more long grass and larger riparian margins alongside the river instead of the more manicured grounds. The River Tone under the M5. © River Tone Lawy says she now asks people to adopt a new perspective. “I want you to think more from an animal perspective,” she tells them. “Rather than us thinking we need to trim that hedge, are we leaving places for birds and insects and all these other species who live here? Are we providing feeding corridors for bats?” Much to her surprise, the group “straightforwardly accepted these insights,” Lawy reports. The larger ambition of ASRA’s experiment is to translate these observations into protective action. Phil Tovey, who co-leads the project with Miguel Castro of UWE, describes the River Tone as a system in which risks compound. For instance, research has found that kestrels living within 30 meters of a major road show elevated cortisol from stress, and they shift from reproduction towards survival. “So when we then look at overall coverage of roads in the region, you can just see the scale of harm, disruption, physical and mental injury that is really widespread,” Tovey concludes. “One of the things that we do in ASRA for a systemic risk response is we look at the underlying structures, the historical conditions and what are the barriers to transformation.” A former Royal Marines Commando, Tovey served on operations across the world, from peacekeeping in Northern Ireland to working with indigenous forces in Afghanistan and deployments across Africa and the Middle East. Before joining ASRA, he worked as the Head of Futures in the U.K.’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs. Rain patters downstream of French Weir. © River Tone He likens the emotional testimonies of the study participants to the shocked reports of civilians caught in war zones. He also conducted roughly two dozen of his own field experiments, switching between species and testing the instructions given to participants. “I’d be going out at four in the morning, roughly knowing where the red deer hang out.” For Tovey, connecting the participants’ testimonies to scientific evidence and a structured framework for mapping risk means “setting the conditions for deeper structural change.” For example, the river and its tributaries contain more than 337 weirs and other obstacles over about 33 kilometers, creating problems for migrating salmon and other creatures. “No one has really considered the density and volume of these pressures on the animals,” Tovey says. “But when I sit as an otter, I see these barriers because as an otter I’m only about six centimeters off the ground.” Conventional assessments tend to divide problems into categories: transport, agriculture, water quality, habitat, biodiversity. Tovey’s digital mapping of the River Tone risks is effectively “bright orange” as different risks overlap. The problem is not merely the number of individual hazards, but their density and interaction. Changing the perspective does not mean abandoning scientific evidence, but it can show which actions will have the most impact. “As a research team, asking a bunch of humans to try and inevitably fail to engage in living as a chosen animal, the absurdity of trying to actually do that was taken really seriously,” says Tovey, addressing the obvious criticism of anthropomorphism. “We never once claimed that Helen was a kestrel, but using the structured process we set out, we need to make an imaginary leap to calibrate what that environment would be like for the animal. Then we start to see barriers in a different way.” The research team briefing the Systemic Risk Assessment. Credit: Darren Honeywell For Lawy, the exercise in changing perspective led to changes in land management, and then to a recognition that she wants to press for changes beyond her local group. “It’s amazing how quickly that local action on a relatively small area can lead you to realize that actually we need some policy changes within the landscape to really make that difference,” she says. The project inspired an even more ambitious question: What does the river need? One of the study participants works in the city council. According to Tovey, “she became instrumental in stitching together the work and applying it to River Tone as a subjective person.” A working group quickly formed, resulting in the adaptation of Somerset’s very first River Rights Charter, which recognizes the river’s rights to regenerate, flow and be protected from harm. Lawy’s stint as a kestrel is part of a growing global movement to shift from an anthropocentric view, inspired by programs such as NYU Law School’s More than Human Life as well as bestselling authors like Charles Foster , whose book Being A Beast portrayed him living as badger, deer, fox and swift. It also marks a return to Indigenous values. In 2008, Indigenous peoples led Ecuador to become the world’s first country to formally recognize the “Rights of Mother Earth,” a ruling that the Global Alliance for the Rights of Nature (GARN) and others subsequently used successfully against a road construction company that dumped rubble into the Vilcabamba River. As a result, the government was forced to clean up the river. Tovey agrees that rivers and other elements of nature should have the right to be represented. “I have never met my MP,” he says. “Yet we accept political representation for humans. What’s problematic is making sure it’s done with integrity.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The approach remains experimental. There are obvious limits to humans attempting to understand other species, and the researchers themselves acknowledge the need for more time. But Tovey hopes to expand ASRA’s work to larger areas. “We have started to forge connections with our sister rivers, reaching out to those groups and thinking about a wider solidarity movement,” Tovey says, intending to integrate the lessons from the River Tone project. Lawy’s experience suggests another potential benefit: changing what people care about. “One of the really important things that’s come out of this for me,” she says, “is the emotional connection that you get back with nature.” That emotional connection is not taken as a substitute for evidence. Rather, it can make evidence harder to ignore. The post The People Who Became Wildlife appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Results-Based Conservation Finance in Africa Gets a $4.6 Million Boost Reading Time: 3 minutes A new $4.6 million commitment from the Rob Walton Foundation is testing whether results-based conservation finance in Africa can tie funding directly to verified outcomes across four protected areas. Results-based conservation finance in Africa took a significant step forward with a new $4.6 million commitment from the Rob Walton Foundation. The funding flows to African Parks, a nonprofit that manages protected areas across the continent. Unlike a typical grant, payment is tied directly to verified conservation outcomes rather than activities alone. The deal relies on a tool called the Verifiable Nature Unit (VNU), which African Parks and The Landbanking Group developed together starting in 2024. Each unit represents one square kilometer of land where ecological integrity has been maintained or improved over a year. Independent verification confirms whether that standard has actually been met before funding is released. Funding under this agreement will support four protected areas spread across very different parts of the continent. Majete Wildlife Reserve in Malawi, Odzala-Kokoua National Park in the Republic of Congo, Garamba National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Zakouma National Park in Chad will all benefit. The money will support biodiversity monitoring, community development projects, and park infrastructure. Each of these four parks faces its own mix of challenges, from poaching pressure to limited local infrastructure and competing land uses nearby. Community development funding is meant to give nearby residents a stake in keeping ecosystems intact, through jobs, services, or shared benefits tied to the park’s success. Supporters of the VNU model argue that linking funding directly to measurable outcomes could eventually make that kind of community investment more consistent across very different park settings. African Parks has already issued VNUs covering a combined 1.37 million hectares across three of these parks in 2025 and 2026. That scale makes the current grant one of the larger tests yet of whether outcomes-based payment can work at a landscape level. Verification and reporting costs are capped at roughly five percent of each park’s management budget, keeping most funding directed at conservation itself. The Rob Walton Foundation’s executive director described VNUs as a way to direct capital toward measurable, verifiable conservation results. He framed the approach as attractive for philanthropy today, while also testing whether it could eventually support other financing tools. Conservation funding gaps across Africa have long hindered efforts to protect large, ecologically important landscapes. Traditional grants often fund activities such as ranger patrols or fencing without directly tying payment to whether wildlife populations or habitat conditions actually improve. Results-based conservation finance in Africa aims to close that gap by making payments conditional on outcomes verified by an independent party. Results-based conservation finance in Africa addresses a long-standing funding gap by making payment conditional on independently verified improvements in wildlife populations and habitat conditions, rather than simply funding ranger patrols or fencing regardless of whether outcomes improve. Photo by Francesco Ungaro on Pexels. Beyond grants, African Parks says the VNU framework could eventually support bonds, credits, and other nature-linked financial instruments. The goal is a standardized metric that investors and donors can trust across very different ecosystems and countries. Conservation finance has often lacked this consistency, with funding mechanisms and reporting standards varying widely by project. African Parks currently manages 24 parks across 13 African countries, which hold an estimated 12 billion tonnes of stored carbon dioxide equivalent. That scale gives the organization a large testing ground for results-based conservation finance in Africa, where a single standardized metric could eventually apply across dozens of ecosystems at once. According to African Parks, VNUs are designed to support a range of financing mechanisms, including pay-for-performance grants, donations, bonds, and credits. The organization’s next steps include reissuing units, expanding the model to more parks, and attracting a wider mix of funders. Whether this approach spreads beyond African Parks will depend on how reliably verification holds up as the model scales, and whether other funders are willing to adopt a similar standard. For now, the Rob Walton Foundation’s commitment offers one of the clearest real-world tests yet of whether results-based conservation finance in Africa can shift funding away from promises and toward outcomes that donors can actually confirm. The post Results-Based Conservation Finance in Africa Gets a $4.6 Million Boost appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: What if a serious spinal defect could be operated on before a baby is born? Doctors at AIIMS Delhi have taken a groundbreaking step towards making that possible! In a first for India, a team of doctors performed an open foetal surgery to repair myelomeningocele, the most severe form of spina bifida, in an unborn baby at 25 weeks of pregnancy. The six-hour operation was performed on 12 November. The condition causes the spinal cord and its protective coverings to protrude through an opening in the spine, potentially leading to paralysis, hydrocephalus and lifelong neurological complications. The milestone was made possible by over five weeks of meticulous planning and the collaboration of more than 30 doctors, nurses and specialists across multiple departments. Even more heartening, the complex procedure was performed free of cost under a government scheme. The mother and baby will continue to receive close medical monitoring throughout the remainder of the pregnancy, delivery and newborn period. A remarkable achievement for Indian healthcare and a huge shoutout to the doctors and medical staff who made it possible! #AIIMSDelhi #FetalSurgery #MedicalBreakthrough #IndianHealthcar #HealthcareHeroes [AIIMS Delhi fetal surgery, India’s first open foetal surgery, spina bifida surgery, myelomeningocele treatment, fetal medicine in India]

items.descriptionOriginal: At 15, when most teenagers were still figuring out their interests, Jai Bhardwaj showed up at his first professional cycling race with little more than determination and a bicycle he had ridden there himself. By the end of the day, he returned home with two bicycles – one he had brought for the race and another he had won. It was a small but defining moment for Jai, one that would shape the rest of his life. Today, at 23, Jai is a national-level cyclist who has represented Delhi in the Cycling Nationals. From competing in road and track cycling championships to guiding aspiring riders through his digital platforms, he is working to encourage more Indians to take up cycling as a serious sport . His journey comes at a time when cycling is gaining greater recognition in the country. With Pune set to host the 105th edition of the UCI Road World Championships in 2032, making India only the fourth Asian country to stage the event, the future of the sport looks promising. For riders like Jai, the championship represents more than an international sporting event coming to India. It offers hope for better opportunities, infrastructure and support for the country's growing cycling community. From his first race at 15 to representing Delhi at Nationals Jai's introduction to cycling was driven by curiosity rather than a structured training programme or professional support. What began as an interest soon developed into a serious pursuit as he began training, participating in races and pushing his limits. His competitive cycling journey began in 2017, when he took part in a Raahgiri Faridabad race at the age of 15. Jai's introduction to cycling was driven by curiosity rather than a structured training programme or professional support. "I wasn't expecting much from the race in which I participated, and thought it would be just another fun ride in the city for an 'awareness campaign,' like how a lot of such events function. "The moment the race started, I flew past almost everyone in the first few moments and crossed the line with a large margin between me and the other finishers. To my surprise, they later revealed that the winners would get a bicycle. I was delighted and felt unreal, and wished I had someone to share the moment with," says Jai. That first win gave him the confidence to pursue cycling more seriously. His parents, too, began recognising his potential and supported him through his training and competitions. Over the years, Jai went on to participate in several private cyclothons, road and track cycling Nationals, state championships and events such as the HCL Cyclothon. In 2019, he finished first at the Gurugram Criterium, secured a top-10 position at the HCL Cyclothon and won the MadoverBiking Cyclothon. He also finished among the top 20 in the U18 Individual Time Trial at the Nationals. These milestones marked his progression from a young participant at a city race to a competitive cyclist representing Delhi at state and national levels in both road and track cycling. For his parents, his first race was the moment when cycling began to feel like more than just a hobby. Seeing him win gave them confidence that he could pursue the sport seriously. A fellow cyclist, Dheeraj Singh, who has closely watched Jai's journey, says his enthusiasm has also inspired others to take up cycling. "Jai began his journey as a cyclist from a young age, and his vibrant and charismatic persona inspired others to cycle too. "He has raced at the national level and uses the experience gained through his competitive cycling journey to help others develop their own cycling techniques. He is an innovative young cyclist who helps his fellow riders improve their cycling performance," says Dheeraj. Using his experience to help more cyclists For Jai, cycling has gradually become about more than personal achievements. He wants to help others understand the sport, improve their performance and make informed choices as they begin their own journeys. Over the years, Jai went on to participate in several private cyclothons, road and track cycling Nationals, state championships and events such as the HCL Cyclothon. To do this, he uses YouTube and Instagram under the handle 'Fast But Faster', where he documents his rides and shares practical information about competitive cycling. His content covers everything from following international cycling races and understanding their rules and regulations to bicycle maintenance, training techniques and choosing the right equipment. He also recommends cycling gear across different budgets, helping aspiring riders understand what they need without spending a fortune. His advice draws on his own experience as a competitive cyclist, including the practical lessons he has learnt through years of training and participating in races. While he has not yet organised formal cycling initiatives or events, his digital content is finding an audience among people interested in the sport. He receives messages and comments from viewers who say his videos have encouraged them to take up cycling or helped them understand the sport better. His contribution also extends to the cycling community around him. According to Dheeraj, Jai is always willing to help fellow riders, whether they need assistance during a ride, have a training-related question or face an equipment issue. He often improvises with his gear and finds practical, do-it-yourself solutions instead of spending a fortune. This resourcefulness is something he also encourages among other cyclists. Having known Jai since his days as a strong young U18 athlete, Dheeraj has watched him progress into a promising U23 cyclist. Making cycling more accessible in India As someone who trains regularly on Indian roads, Jai understands the importance of creating a safer and more supportive environment for cyclists. His training often involves hours of riding, usually early in the morning to avoid peak traffic. He believes that greater awareness among motorists, dedicated cycling lanes and better road conditions can make a significant difference to the experience of cyclists. An accident reinforced his belief in the need for safer roads and better infrastructure for cyclists. Sharing some of the challenges riders encounter, he explains, "It's a survival game on the roads in India. If you go out for a zone two heart rate training ride in the city, there is a 100 percent chance you'll unintentionally cross your heart rate zone because of the overwhelming traffic stimuli, constant honking, and chaos everywhere, all of which naturally spike your heart rate. Dust is another massive problem, besides the already infamous AQI. I clean my bicycle almost every night before heading out, and I end up with a very fine layer of dust all over me by the time I return home. Now imagine how much of this dust enters your body during exercise." For Jai, greater exposure to professional cycling can help address another challenge: the perception that cycling is merely a recreational activity. "When I used to mention that I do cycling as a sport in my school, people used to think that pro-cycling means leisurely street riding. I believe the sheer reason for that is a lack of exposure and awareness. There is no proper support for local grassroots-level athletes, cycling infrastructure, and overall safety. However, with the recent success of the Bajaj Pune Grand Tour 2026, I believe that things are changing," he says. He believes that regular broadcasts of professional cycling races, with commentary in multiple languages, could help more Indians understand and follow the sport. Conducting regular competitive events that are not merely profit-seeking cyclothons, providing financial assistance to young cyclists and organising school visits to cycling events are some of the other measures he suggests. Returning to the road after an accident Like many athletes, Jai's journey has also involved setbacks. One of the most challenging moments came when an accident left him with a severe lip injury. The incident required him to pause and focus on recovery, both physically and mentally. For his family, it was a difficult experience, particularly because of the risks associated with training on busy Indian roads. "Indian roads are quite dangerous and aren't really meant for cycling . Indian professional cyclists are very few in number when compared to those abroad. We have seen him get hurt when he was hit by a car, so we are really scared now. Whenever he goes out, we remain worried until he returns home. The downside of this sport is that it is a very physically vulnerable sport," say his parents. However, cycling remained an important part of Jai's life. He gradually returned to riding, rebuilding his confidence with every outing. The experience also reinforced his belief in the need for safer roads and better infrastructure for cyclists. Building a stronger cycling culture for the next generation Jai's aspirations extend beyond his own competitive journey. He hopes to see more young Indians discover cycling, access professional training and get opportunities to compete. He believes that identifying talent at the grassroots level is an important starting point. Professional cycling requires years of dedicated training and considerable financial investment, which can make it difficult for young athletes to pursue the sport. Sponsorships for promising cyclists could help ease these costs, while academic support from schools and colleges would allow student athletes to balance their education with training. He also hopes to see stronger enforcement of road-safety rules, dedicated cycling infrastructure and greater awareness among motorists. For Jai, making cycling more accessible means creating an environment in which young riders can discover the sport and pursue it without being held back by a lack of information, financial resources or opportunities. His parents, who have supported him since his first race, see his contribution to cycling as extending beyond his own achievements. They take pride in the way he shares his knowledge and encourages other riders. From winning his first bicycle at 15 to representing Delhi at national championships and building a digital platform to guide aspiring cyclists, Jai continues to find ways to contribute to a sport he is passionate about. And as India prepares to welcome one of the world's biggest cycling events in 2032, young riders like him are helping build the interest and awareness that could give the sport a stronger future in the country. Follow Jai Bhardwaj's cycling journey and find more tips on: YouTube: Fast But Faster Instagram: @fastbutfaster
