Διαβάστε το πρωτότυπο άρθρο εδώ. Το γυαλί ως υλικό είναι γεμάτο αντιφάσεις. Ανάλογα με…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article was written by Suzanne Peck , a lecturer of art at the Rochester Institute of Technology, for The Conversation — a nonprofit news organization dedicated to sharing the knowledge of researchers and scientists, under a Creative Commons license . Read the original article here . Glass as a material is full of contradictions. Depending on the form and use, glass can be fragile or strong, opaque or transparent, rough or smooth. The studios my colleagues and I teach and learn in, as glass instructors, echo this abundance of physical opposites. These environments are simultaneously immersive, complex, seductive, and demanding. When the studio is in action, you might hear glass breaking, hot metal being quenched in water, glassblowing pipes rolling on the workbench rails, and some good tunes on the stereo. You might smell hot beeswax and burning newspaper. You might feel a bit of waste glass under your shoe or the intense heat from the furnaces and a breeze from a well-placed fan. Glassblowers learn to listen, to feel, and to find some focus within and among the kinetic. The constant stimuli of the glass studio may not seem anything like a sterile science lab, and yet glass artists need to accrue knowledge of physics and chemistry to achieve any kind of control with this dynamic material. They must choose a material with the desired properties and during the process judge factors such as heat and malleability. Glass as a Material At Rochester Institute of Technology, where I help run the glass program, we primarily use two types of glasses. In our hot glass studio we melt “soft” glass . This glass is specifically formulated to be melted in a furnace and used by the glassblower. It’s a combination of fine mesh silica sand, soda ash, and lime, with small amounts of a few additional ingredients that keep the glass beautiful when it’s at its top temperature of 2,200 degrees Fahrenheit (1,204 degrees Celsius). In our flameworking studio, we use a borosilicate glass . You might recognize this glass as the brand Pyrex made in Corning, New York. This is a super heat-resistant glass. It melts at a higher temperature than soft glass and arrives to our students in preformed rods that they can melt and shape by torch in our flameworking studio. The differences in chemistry really change how these glasses look and behave. Picofluidicist/Wikimedia Commons Pyrex cookware is made out of a specially formulated, heat-resistant type of glass called borosilicate. Glass, from a material science perspective, is categorized as an amorphous solid , meaning that glass’s molecules are arranged in a near-random pattern and there is no sharp melting point . Rather, glass gradually softens over a wide temperature range. Gathering Glass Once you’ve adjusted to the chaos of the studio, it’s time to start working. We have two furnaces in our hot glass studio, where we work with soft glass, so anytime during the school year there is between 700 to 1,200 pounds of glass. It’s kept in the furnace at its molten state (2,200 degrees F or 1,204 degrees C), ready to be gathered and transformed. AP Photo/Keith Srakocic Glass artists heat up their glass in a furnace so that it’s molten and easy to mold. When we work with the material, transforming it with tools and breath and heat, it needs to be kept in a workable heat zone — probably between 1,100 and 2,000 F (593 and 1,094 C). When the glass dips below that range, we perceive it as solid, though at the molecular level it is still dynamic and acting more like a liquid. To make anything — a sculpture, a tumbler, a celestial magical orb, or a pumpkin — you start by gathering glass out of the furnace on a metal rod. Once you’ve gathered your glass, you start making decisions. Elizabeth Lamark/RIT An artist works in the Glass Hot Shop at RIT. When glass is in its molten state, the artist can shape it and blow into it. You might ask yourself: What tools do I need to begin to shape and transform this glass into the object I have in mind? If you wait too long and the glass begins cooling down, you’ll need to reheat it to reintroduce malleability , allowing you to continue working it without breaking it. A big part of glasswork is moving between the reheating chamber and the bench, where the artist uses tools to move and stretch the molten glass into the desired shape. You’ll need to alternate between these two stations many times. Glassblowing is a team activity. I have physical and intellectual support from my colleagues: breath from their lungs, protection from the heat, additional bits of glass brought from the furnace to add to my object. We almost never work alone. So, say I want to make a very basic clear tumbler. This is a simple conceptual object — utilitarian, domestic, and intimate. It is also a tricky one to make well: too heavy and it feels bad in the hand, too thick at the lip and it dribbles when you drink, too thin at the bottom and it will break before it is complete. Maybe I want to design it so it is slightly conical: wider at the bottom than the top, so it’s less likely to tip over. Maybe I want it to have a little indent for the user’s thumb as a gentle invitation to her hand. First I make my design: I draw it. I share it with my team so they can predict the process and the object’s needs. Then we begin. Working With Physics I gather glass out of the furnace, let it cool a bit, then introduce a bubble in the glass by blowing into the pipe, the hollow rod that attaches to the object I’m making. I reheat, sit at the bench, and begin to shape the glass using both gravity and the Jills, a cooling and shaping tool. The Jills is kind of like a large pair of tongs. It hasn’t changed much in design for 2,000 years. AP Photo/Gerry Broome Glass artists use a variety of tools to shape their work. I ask for some air from my teammate, and she blows into the pipe while I’m shaping the glass. The bubble transforms into a pill shape, slightly wider at the bottom. I constrict the area right in front of the pipe. I’m focusing on shape and heat, taking care to not let the glass get too cold. If the glass drops to about 1,000 F (538 C), it enters a danger zone. If it’s not yet finished, it needs to be warmed up in the reheating chamber; or if it is done, put away in a kiln to cool slowly. If glass cools too quickly, the molecules freeze into a chaotic pattern, which causes stresses that result in fracture. To combat this volatility, when the glass object is done and ready to be cooled, we place the object in an annealer : a kiln set to a resting temperature of 930 F (500 C). This temperature is like a Goldilocks zone for our glass: It’s not so hot that the glass will deform, but not so cool that the glass will stress and break. Once the kilns are full, a computer guide takes them down to room temperature over about 10 hours. As I continue to work on my cup, I get more heat, focusing on the very end of the bubble — the part that will be the base of the cup. I then sit down and have another member of my team flatten the bottom with a wooden paddle while I tool the glass with the Jills to keep its shape. The cycle continues on and on. The process is quick, but also there are so many little steps that it would take nearly a full-length book to describe them all. When asked how long it takes to make a tumbler, I’ll often answer, “About 10 years or 10 minutes, depending on how you think about time and material knowledge.” This is both glib and true. Glass demands attention, dedication, and a willingness to make connections between physics and chemistry and your observable experiences. It is a highly challenging and equally rewarding material to work with and alongside. I count myself very lucky. Κανένας κολυμβητής δεν το άφησε εκεί. Όπως τα περισσότερα από αυτά που συλλέγονται στις πιο δυσπρόσιτες ακτές της Ελλάδας, οδήγησε i…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM At some point in the past three decades, a beer can printed with a Spanish-language ad for a 1990s World Cup washed up on Patroklos, a small islet in the Saronic Gulf about 65 nautical miles (75 miles) from Athens. No swimmer left it there. Like most of what collects on Greece’s harder-to-reach shores, it rode in on the currents, and it stayed until a crew working on a Greek coastline cleanup picked it up, sorted it, and wrote it down. That last step, the writing down, is what makes this project more interesting than a beach sweep. Every bottle, net, and wrapper the crew logs becomes a clue about where the Mediterranean’s waste starts its trip. A Greek coastline cleanup run from the sea The Typhoon and its 20-person crew Greece has the longest coastline of any Mediterranean country, and much of it has no road leading to it. Since July 2019, the Typhoon Project has reached those stretches by water, using a 72-meter (236-foot) ship as its base. Each day, a crew of 20 heads ashore in five inflatable boats and gathers, sorts, and records between 500 and 1,000 kilograms (roughly 1,100 to 2,200 pounds) of waste, which then goes to the appropriate facilities for recycling. The project belongs to the Public Benefit Foundation Athanassios C. Laskaridis , a Greek foundation whose work centers on protecting the environment and the sea in particular. By February 2023, the crew had completed its first full circuit of the islands and most of the mainland coast. Seven years, 1,140 tonnes Across more than 10,000 cleanup operations, the Typhoon has removed 1,140 tonnes (about 1,257 US tons) of trash. Peggy Xirotagarou, the foundation’s executive director, has learned that the number means more to people as an image than as a weight. “To help people picture it in their minds, we are talking about 22 Olympic-size swimming pools or around 1160 large containers,” she said. Marine litter as a research record Counting every item on every beach The cleanup is half the job. The other half happens after the bags are on board, when the crew records what was found, item by item and beach by beach. Thanasis Besios, who manages the Typhoon Project, considers that record as valuable as the cleared sand. “One part of the project is collecting the waste, but the second is collecting the data. We carry out detailed recording of all the waste. We know exactly what quantity there is, how many kilos, how many items from each beach. At the moment we have the largest database on marine pollution in the Mediterranean, and we are developing it every day,” he told Euronews. Researchers are putting that record to use. The project works with the Laboratory of Marine Geology and Physical Oceanography at the University of Patras to study waste on the seabed of the Saronic and Thermaic Gulfs, and with the Marine Remote Sensing Research Group at the University of the Aegean, which uses remote sensing technology to locate and map plastics. Tracing coastal pollution back inland The Cyclone program Seven years of sorting led the foundation to an uncomfortable conclusion about its own beaches. Plenty of what lands on the coast was never thrown into the sea in the first place, and illegal, unmanaged landfills are still running in many parts of Greece. “By observing the waste we were finding on the shores, we realised that a large proportion came from inland,” Xirotagarou said. The foundation’s response, launched in 2024, is a land-based counterpart called Cyclone . “It involves large-scale clean-ups in lakes, rivers and archaeological sites. We have created three large teams in different parts of Greece, where every day we collect more than 1,000 kilos of waste,” she said. Schools on every stop Wherever the Typhoon drops anchor, the team also visits local schools, then brings students out to the shoreline. Xirotagarou sees the classroom work as the long game behind the whole operation. “Because that is the ultimate goal. For them to become responsible citizens and for this reckless use of single-use plastics to stop,” she said. A project that began by picking up after the sea has ended up asking where the trash started. A crew can clear an islet in an afternoon, but slowing what reaches it depends on the steadier work the foundation has added since 2024, from the river and lake crews to the classroom visits. The Greek coastline cleanup will keep finding cans like the one on Patroklos, though its logbook now gives Greece a much clearer sense of which ones drifted in from abroad and which started a few miles inland. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Very few Americans have ever eaten foie gras. It’s a niche luxury, served mostly in high-end restaurants, and yet on November 3 it produced some of the most lopsided results of the night in two American cities. In Washington, DC, 73 percent of voters backed a ban on selling the force-fed duck liver, and in Denver, 66 percent did. They weren’t alone. Across this year’s midterms , animal welfare ballot measures had a strong showing, and the pattern in what passed and what didn’t says something about how voters approach animals when the question in front of them is narrow and specific. Foie gras bans win by wide margins How foie gras is produced Foie gras comes from ducks that are force-fed through a metal pipe about 60 times in the final weeks before slaughter, until their livers swell to six to 10 times their natural size. Producers and many fine-dining chefs maintain that the practice is harmless, or at least no worse than other factory farming methods, while veterinary research has concluded it can be quite painful for the birds. DC and Denver join a growing list “Tonight DC decided that force-feeding a bird has no place here,” said Cady Witt of Pro-Animal DC, the group that put the measure on the ballot. The District’s ban on sales takes effect in July 2027 . California, New York City, Pittsburgh, and Portland, Oregon, already restrict foie gras sales, though the earlier city bans came from officials rather than voters, according to Ballotpedia . Outside the U.S., more than 20 European countries prohibit foie gras production; Brazil banned both its sale and production this year, and India has barred imports since 2014. Producers and chefs plan to fight back The votes may not be the last word. A representative from Hudson Valley Farms, the country’s largest foie gras producer, told Axios the company is considering legal challenges. In DC, Bart Hutchins, chef and owner of the restaurant Butterworth’s, wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he was “incredibly disappointed” the measure reached the ballot, The Hill reported , and he has since hosted four-course foie gras dinners to raise money for a possible lawsuit. Colorado rejects a constitutional hunting amendment What Amendment 83 asked voters Colorado’s Amendment 83 would have written “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” into the state constitution and named hunting and fishing as the preferred way to manage wildlife populations. About 55 percent of voters opposed it, according to unofficial results . Supporters argued that hunting and fishing rights shouldn’t depend on statutes or on whoever sits on the state wildlife commission, and 24 states already have some version of the protection in their constitutions. The amendment also exempted nongame and endangered species. Why “traditional methods” mattered Hunting and fishing are already protected by Colorado statute, so critics focused on the phrase “traditional methods.” “Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, told Vox in October. Colorado currently bans those practices. Vox reporter Neel Dhanesha described the stakes for animals that were never the intended target: “Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf , and a lynx.” Opponents also worried that naming hunting the preferred management tool could sideline alternatives such as wildlife birth control and relocation. Where voters drew the line on animal welfare Conservation funding passes in several states Wildlife habitat did well this year too. Massachusetts voters approved a measure to fund nature conservation, and voters in Brevard County, Florida, renewed a tax that pays for manatee and dolphin habitat restoration. Conservation measures in Arkansas and Rhode Island also passed. Broader bans have a harder time Not every animal measure finds a majority. In 2024, Denver voters turned down a ban on fur sales, which drew 42.4 percent support, and a ban on slaughterhouses within city limits, which drew 36.3 percent, according to Ballotpedia. Set beside this year’s foie gras results, the two votes suggest that measures targeting one specific practice tend to fare better than ones that would reshape a whole industry. Farm animal laws and the candidates who opposed them Several candidate races also touched on animal welfare policy. In 2016, Massachusetts voters banned the sale of eggs and pork from hens and pregnant pigs kept in small cages, and California voters passed a nearly identical law two years later. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas and Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa, both Republicans, have sponsored bills to override those state laws, most recently the Save Our Bacon Act, and both lost their races this year. In Colorado’s Eighth Congressional District, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a state lawmaker and former Earthjustice attorney who sued meat companies over pollution, defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans. In Iowa, Chris Jones, a water quality expert who campaigned on cleaning up livestock and farm pollution, narrowly lost his bid for agriculture secretary. Neither major party has made animal welfare a central campaign issue, but the results will shape how these debates play out in Congress and statehouses over the next two years. For the campaigners in DC, the win came down to thousands of individual signatures and votes, a slow, ground-level way of changing what a city allows on its menus. Witt closed her statement on election night by thanking the people who did that work: “Thank you to everyone who signed the petition and voted to make DC a kinder place for animals.” Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: The bots roll along blood vessels to stir up stagnant blood and push drugs toward clots. Drugs that break up blood clots are vital for treating strokes, heart attacks, and clogged blood vessels in the lungs, but sometimes blockages are so large that medication struggles to get through. Now, researchers are building tiny magnetic robots to help medicines reach their targets. Severe blockages in blood vessels pose a tricky problem. The bloodstream is the only way to deliver clot-busting drugs, but if a clot stops the flow, there is no other way to carry them there. A team at ETH Zurich in Switzerland has a workaround. Magnetically driven microbots that roll along vessel walls can stir up stagnant blood so the drug gets pushed towards the clot. In lab tests, the approach dissolved clots six times faster than with the drug alone, and in experiments on pigs, it restored blood flow to an area twice as large after 30 minutes. “To our knowledge, we are the first to show in a clinically relevant large-animal model that the use of microrobots in this way does indeed enhance thrombolysis [the process of dissolving blood clots],” Schürle said in a press release . The bots are a far cry from your traditional robot. Just eight micrometers long, each is shaped like a grain of rice and made of a sugar-based polymer laced with magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles. During fabrication, the researchers expose the devices to a rotating magnetic field that pushes the nanoparticles into a straight line, essentially creating a bar magnet running the length of each bot. When a magnetic control system outside the body applies a rotating field, the internal magnet spins and causes each bot to tumble head over tail. The bots themselves don’t carry drugs. Rather, they’re released near a blockage along with clot-busting medicine. As the bots roll along the vessel walls towards the restriction, they create currents that carry the drug into the clot. To test the approach, the team built an artificial network of vessel-like channels and plugged it with clots made of pig blood. They compared what happened when they added the clot-dissolving drug alone to what happened when they added the drug and the bots together. Adding the bots cleared the clots six times faster than when they tried just the drug. To see if the strategy would work in real biological systems, the team blocked arteries in live pigs and treated them with just drugs and drugs plus microbots. After 30 minutes, the area with restored blood flow was twice as large in animals that received the bots. The work adds to a growing body of research into clot-busting magnetic microrobots. Last year, a separate ETH Zurich team led by Bradley Nelson published a paper in Science describing a dissolvable gel capsule that could be steered through blood vessels and release a clot-dissolving drug when heated by a high-frequency magnetic field. Others have taken a more mechanical approach. Researchers at the University of Twente and Radboud University Medical Center in the Netherlands used 3D-printed, screw-shaped robots containing tiny magnets to drill into clots, removing enough material from a blocked artery taken from a sheep to get blood flowing again. While the ETH team have filed a patent application for their bots, it’s still early. The paper describing the results has yet to clear peer review, and human trials are a long way off. Nonetheless, the results are another indication that microrobots could one day become a valuable new tool in a doctor’s arsenal. The post Tiny Magnetic Robots Help Dissolve Blood Clots Six Times Faster Than With Drugs Alone appeared first on SingularityHub .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice Reading Time: 3 minutes Mushroom coffins and green burial options let families return nutrients to the soil. Mushroom coffins and green burial options give families a new way to care for the planet. Loop Biotech , a company in Delft, the Netherlands, grows these products from living mushroom roots. The company says traditional funerals can harm the environment. It points to cutting old trees, releasing carbon dioxide, and adding toxic chemicals to soil. Loop Biotech wants to offer a gentler choice. Interest in greener funerals is growing. A 2023 report from the National Funeral Directors Association found that 60% of consumers would explore green funeral options. That is about six in every ten people, so mushroom coffins and green burials meet a real demand. The idea began at Delft University of Technology. Founders Bob and Lonneke Hendrikx were graduating there when they asked a simple question: Could a final act help the earth instead of harming it? They found an answer in mycelium, the root network of mushrooms. It grows underground and breaks down dead plant matter. As it does, it releases nutrients that feed new life. Mycelium is known as one of nature’s biggest recyclers. Researchers have only recently given it close attention. For years, many of them focused on plants and animals above ground. Loop Biotech grows its products from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers. Upcycled means the fibers are reused instead of thrown away. Hemp is a tough plant often used for rope and cloth. The growing process takes just seven days. Trees used for traditional coffins can take many decades to grow. That difference shows how quickly this material can be made. Once the coffin is buried, it begins to break down. The company says it biodegrades in about 45 days. Mushroom coffins and green burial materials like these return to the soil faster than most wood and metal. The coffin is also strong. Hendrikx says it can carry about 440 pounds (200 kilograms). He adds that people are often surprised by how soft and sturdy it feels. The company invented the world’s first mushroom coffin, called the Loop Living Cocoon. It also makes the Loop EarthRise and the Loop ForestBed. The company describes its products as patented and award-winning. Mushroom coffins and green burial options now include the Loop EarthRise, the world’s first urn made from mushrooms, grown in seven days from local mushrooms and upcycled hemp fibers to nourish the earth and grow a tree in your memory. Photo courtesy of Loop Biotech . Each product is 100% natural and biodegradable. Biodegradable means it breaks down naturally over time. The company also says its products enrich the soil. Soil-enriching is a bold claim, so families should look at the details. Asking a funeral provider about materials, local rules, and cemetery policies is a smart first step. Green burial is a broader movement. It generally avoids embalming chemicals and uses naturally biodegradable materials. Mushroom coffins and green burial fit together because both aim to leave the ground healthier. Why does this matter to families? Many people want a funeral that matches how they lived. For someone who loved gardens or forests, a soil-enriching option may feel personal. Loop Biotech describes its approach as working with nature rather than against it. The founders chose living organisms over dead materials. That idea shapes every product the company grows. The founders describe their mission as turning endings into new beginnings. This view invites people to think about death differently. It treats a funeral as part of a natural cycle. The company grows its products at a facility in Delft, close to where the founders studied. Local mushrooms keep the process tied to the region. That choice also supports the company’s goal of a positive footprint. A footprint is the mark people leave on the environment. The company wants that mark to be positive. It aims to return nutrients to the soil. Demand is spreading beyond Europe. Hendrikx estimates it has sold more than 2,000 coffins in Europe and has started selling in North America. Mushroom coffins and green burial alternatives are now reaching families on both continents. The company shares a brand video. It tells the story behind the products and the people who make them. For more detail, people can watch a TEDx talk by Bob Hendrikx. TEDx is an independently organized event that follows the TED talk format. He explains how mycelium works, how the products grow in seven days, and his vision of a regenerative world that restores natural systems. Mushroom coffins are one of several ideas for gentler goodbyes. Families are also finding new ways to honor loved ones while protecting the planet. Choosing a funeral involves many feelings and practical questions. Families who want an earth-friendly path now have more to consider. Mushroom coffins and green burial may help more people leave a positive mark. The post Mushroom Coffins and Green Burial Give Families a Soil-Enriching Choice appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
items.description: Είμαι Τρίτη πρωί στο Against Da Grain, ένα κουρείο σε έναν ήσυχο δρόμο στη North Shore του Staten Island. Ο ιδιοκτήτης Σον Γουάιτ ολοκληρώνει την περικοπή για έναν μεσήλικα μαύρο ενώ ένας άλλος πελάτης περιμένει εκεί κοντά. Γύρω τους, οι κομμωτές εργάζονται μέσω μιας ροής πελατών. οι συζητήσεις κινούνται μεταξύ αστείων, κοινωνικών ζητημάτων και συνηθισμένων προβλημάτων — α…
items.descriptionOriginal: I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says. The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives. Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how comfortable they were discussing intimate concerns — and how closely they listened to their barber. “It’s been said to me many times that many Black men trust their barber more than they trust their doctor,” he says. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] CLIP sought to build on that familiarity as a way to reach people with undiagnosed hypertension. The condition is both common and easy to miss. About six in 10 non-Hispanic Black men in the United States have hypertension, according to federal data. Yet high blood pressure often produces no symptoms. Among men ages 18 to 39 who have hypertension, the federal data found, fewer than one in four know they have it . Routine access to health care can make early detection more likely, but access is only part of the problem. A 2019 study linked medical mistrust and perceived racism in health care with delayed checkups and blood-pressure screening among Black men. “It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” says Sean White. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Led by NYU Langone in partnership with Community Health Action of Staten Island (CHASI), CLIP brought blood-pressure screening and health support into 22 Black-owned barbershops from Staten Island zip codes with high hypertension prevalence . Against Da Grain was one of them. W hite’s appointments that Tuesday often stretched beyond 30 minutes. “The barber chair is perfectly set up for measuring blood pressure,” Ravenell says. Some patients experience what’s known as “white coat syndrome,” meaning the stress of a clinical setting causes their blood pressure to rise temporarily. By contrast, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened, so with proper technique, a reading taken at the barber shop may better reflect their usual levels. The challenge, Ravenell adds, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Unlike in a clinical setting, getting a haircut gives someone time to sit and grow comfortable before being screened. Credit: Tolu Olasoji During CLIP, local Black male community health workers measured patrons’ blood pressure, counseled them, and connected them with medical and social services. Barbers encouraged customers to participate, but screenings were offered without pressure. “I allowed the men to decide whether they wanted to engage with me,” says a community health worker. Importantly, the community health workers were often themselves customers at the participating barbershops and knew the barbers and customers. Ravenell says that familiarity meant “their presence is not an intrusion, as it might be for someone with a white coat.” Across the program, 636 men were screened. Four hundred sixty-one were found to have elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension, 430 of whom enrolled in the study. Participants were 38 years old on average; only 24 percent reported having a primary care provider, and about half had health insurance. The study followed up with enrolled men at six-month intervals through 18 months, even after recruitment at individual shops had ended. At 18 months, community health workers obtained a repeat blood-pressure reading from 96 percent of participants. That level of follow-up, Ravenell says, is unusual and difficult to achieve in a long-running study. Dr. Chidinma Ibe, a community health workers researcher at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Equity, calls the figures “extremely, extremely impressive,” adding that they reinforce the value of meeting people where they are. D espite these successes, however, CLIP did not produce the primary result researchers had hoped for . At 12 months, participants’ systolic blood pressure had changed little. Fewer men met the study’s definition of incident stage two hypertension at 12 months, but the difference was no longer statistically significant at 18 months. Dr. Ibe says that given that the intervention was among men with elevated blood pressure or untreated stage one hypertension rather than severely uncontrolled disease, the limited movement in its main blood-pressure outcome was “not terribly surprising.” The challenge for CLIP, notes Dr. Joseph Ravenell, was to “leverage what’s special about the barbershop without ruining what’s special about the barbershop.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji For Derek Griffith, a University of Pennsylvania professor who studies Black men’s health, success in simply reaching men is separate from controlling their blood pressure. He says the major determinants of blood-pressure control remain in what men experience outside both barbershops and clinical care. Dr. Idris Robinson, research project manager for Penn’s Program for Research on Men’s Health, likewise cautions against treating the barbershop itself as the intervention. “The blood pressure outcomes weren’t rooted in some magical equation where barbers plus Black men equals guaranteed improvements in Black men’s health,” he says. Sustained engagement, he argues, also depends on collaboration among academic and community partners, barbers’ relationships with clients, and a wider support network. “That infrastructure is critical.” That becomes crucial after an elevated reading. When this occurred with CLIP participants, community health workers explained what the number could mean and encouraged medical follow-up. When it came to a referral, notes Joseph Ebron, CHASI’s director of health equity, “We would let them know what we offer, but it was up to them to take it.” Credit: Tolu Olasoji Even when people wanted help, navigating existing services could complicate the handoff. Workers sometimes met people who thought they lacked coverage, only to discover they were already enrolled elsewhere but were not getting the help they needed. And because they were already attached to another provider or organization, CHASI could not always simply move them into a different service. “We can’t just, like, snatch them,” says Ebron. Ibe points to a structural problem behind that handoff: the fragmented American health care system. Insurance issues, the absence of an established primary care relationship, and weak connections between community organizations and clinical teams can all interrupt the route to care. “If the [community health worker] isn’t employed by that clinic, there’s only so much they can do,” she says. Sustaining even the community side required labor. Active recruitment through Against Da Grain lasted about two months. “We did it for some time without receiving any type of payments,” says White, adding that the program brought “a lot of extra work.” CHASI adapted around the business in real-time: For instance, Ebron says to work around Against Da Grain’s preferences, they screened outside, where workers could pull up a small mobile health unit and barbers could direct interested customers to it. Workers learned to take up less space, getting rid of tables and flyers in favor of a simpler setup: a blood-pressure monitor and materials carried in a bag. Though CLIP is now over, there are larger screening events every two to three months and health workers can return to shops when requested. Credit: Tolu Olasoji Ravenell sees funding — and therefore sustainability — as the broader limitation. When CLIP ended in September 2025, he says Staten Island screening partners continued some services “essentially pro bono” during a funding gap. His team has since received two new NIH grants to build on CLIP’s infrastructure and train community health workers to screen in barbershops for diabetes and diabetic eye disease. For now, CLIP itself is over, though Ebron says CHASI conducts larger screening events every two to three months and can return to shops when requested. Whether the model can travel is another question. Ravenell says Staten Island had an advantage before CLIP began: CHASI had already spent more than 30 years working in the borough through community health workers. “Replicated, yes, easily, no,” Ebron says, because success depends on what already exists locally. CLIP reinforced White’s sense of responsibility to the community he has served for more than 35 years, while sharpening his awareness of the health concerns moving through it. “It helped me realize how many people have elevated levels,” he says. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime Around noon at Against Da Grain, White’s final appointment brings in a young couple and their son, there for the boy’s first haircut. His mother livestreams the occasion to relatives. When the boy climbs down, his father takes his place in the chair. One generation giving way to another, if only for a haircut. items.titleOriginal: The Cozy Emergence of Repair Cafés
items.description: Στα υπόγεια των εκκλησιών και στις κοινοτικές αίθουσες, οι Αμερικανοί συγκεντρώνονται όχι μόνο για να επισκευάσουν σπασμένες λάμπες και ραγισμένες καρέκλες, αλλά για να απωθήσουν μια οικονομία που επωφελείται από τη μοναξιά και τη σπατάλη. Όταν η Lilly Pettus έφερε μια καρέκλα τραπεζαρίας -- μετακόμισε σε έξι πολιτείες για τριάντα χρόνια, κρατώντας στο ξύλο της το βάρος του οικογενειακού γέλιου και της σκληρής συνέλευσης…
items.descriptionOriginal: Across church basements and community halls, Americans are gathering not just to fix broken lamps and cracked chairs, but to push back against an economy that profits from loneliness and waste. When Lilly Pettus brought a dining room chair -- moved across six states over thirty years, holding in its wood the weight of family laughter and hard conversations -- to a repair caf in Decatur, Georgia, she left with something more than a mended joint: strangers' hands had pressed her family's history back together. "When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it's very lonely," says Martine Postma, who founded Repair Caf International in 2010, and the repair caf s she helped seed around the world are a quiet argument against that loneliness. In neighborhoods where the need is economic as much as environmental, and in ones where it is sentimental, the impulse turns out to be the same: a refusal to let things, and the connections they carry, be so easily discarded. What these gatherings reveal, almost incidentally, is that the skills of care have never really disappeared; they've just been waiting for a place to gather.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries Reading Time: 3 minutes Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide have expanded from a single German packaging rule in 1991 into a global compliance landscape spanning more than 70 countries today. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide shift the financial and physical burden of waste management from governments and taxpayers to the companies that manufacture and sell products. Under these laws, producers must collect, recycle, and properly dispose of the packaging and products they put on the market, fundamentally changing the economics of how goods are designed and sold. The concept traces back to Germany’s Packaging Ordinance of 1991, the world’s first EPR regulation. At the time, packaging waste accounted for roughly half of landfill volume and a third of total waste in Germany, pushing national landfill capacity toward its limits and forcing policymakers to act. More than three decades later, extended producer responsibility laws worldwide have evolved from that single national response into one of the most significant regulatory trends reshaping global manufacturing and retail. Europe remains the most mature region for these frameworks, with approximately 40 to 45 countries now operating established EPR schemes. The European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, which entered into force in February 2025 and applies fully from August 2026, replaced the previous directive with uniform, directly applicable requirements across all member states. The regulation requires packaging to meet EU recyclability performance criteria, sets recycled-content targets for plastic packaging starting in 2030, and restricts PFAS in food-contact packaging starting in August 2026. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide increasingly extend beyond packaging alone. France’s framework, codified in its Environmental Code in 1992, now covers packaging, paper, textiles, electrical and electronic equipment, and batteries, with industrial and commercial packaging added to the scope in January 2025. This expansion reflects a broader pattern: once EPR infrastructure exists for one product category, governments frequently extend similar accountability to additional waste streams. In Asia, Japan’s Container and Packaging Recycling Law dates to 1997, obligating producers to fund recycling for designated packaging materials, while recent circular economy obligations have supplemented rather than replaced that core framework. South Korea operates what is widely considered one of the strictest EPR systems globally under its Resource Circulation Act, requiring companies to reduce packaging weight, improve recyclability, and submit to public disclosure of violators as a reputational enforcement mechanism alongside heavy fines. Extended Producer Responsibility laws worldwide increasingly rely on eco-modulated fees that reward recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed packaging, creating market pressure for companies across Europe, Asia, and the Americas to redesign products proactively rather than simply absorbing compliance costs. Photo by Mikhail Nilov on Pexels. China’s approach folds extended producer responsibility obligations into its broader Law on Prevention and Control of Environmental Pollution by Solid Waste, expanding registration and recycling reporting requirements for both electronics and packaging sectors. India’s Plastic Waste Rules, first introduced in 2016 and amended in 2022, require producers, importers, and brand owners to register and take direct responsibility for collecting, recycling, or disposing of plastic packaging waste they introduce into the market. Extended producer responsibility laws worldwide show particularly rapid momentum across the Americas. In Canada, most provinces are fully transitioning to EPR models for packaging and printed paper, requiring registration with provincial programs, annual reporting by material type and weight, and payment of eco-modulated fees that vary by packaging performance and recyclability. Brazil’s National Policy on Solid Waste requires manufacturers, importers, distributors, and sellers to implement reverse-logistics systems that ensure packaging is reused or recycled rather than discarded. Chile’s Law 20.920 similarly requires producers of priority products to establish their own collection, recovery, and recycling schemes to meet government-set targets. In the United States, more than half a dozen states have already implemented EPR legislation, with additional states expected to follow as the model gains bipartisan traction. This state-by-state approach creates a patchwork of overlapping requirements that producers selling nationally must navigate simultaneously. Beyond mandatory frameworks, some nations have pursued voluntary or co-regulatory pathways as stepping stones toward fuller accountability. Australia’s National Packaging Targets, administered by the Australian Packaging Covenant Organization, aim for 100% of packaging to be recyclable, reusable, or compostable and operate through industry-led stewardship rather than direct government mandate. New Zealand has introduced voluntary EPR initiatives for packaging, with mandatory requirements expected as the voluntary phase matures. A common thread across extended producer responsibility laws worldwide is eco-modulated fee structures, financial penalties or incentives tied directly to how recyclable, reusable, or sustainably designed a product’s packaging is. This design creates market pressure encouraging companies to redesign packaging proactively rather than simply paying compliance costs passively, since better-designed packaging typically carries lower fees under most EPR schemes. For companies operating or distributing products internationally, this patchwork of national and regional requirements creates genuine compliance complexity. Registration requirements, reporting formats, fee structures, and penalty regimes vary significantly by country, even as the underlying principle that producers bear responsibility for their products’ end-of-life impact remains consistent across jurisdictions. As extended producer responsibility laws worldwide continue expanding into new product categories and new countries, the regulatory trajectory points firmly in one direction: toward holding manufacturers accountable not just for what they sell, but for what eventually becomes of it, transforming waste management from a public cost into a cost of doing business built directly into product design and corporate strategy. The post Extended Producer Responsibility Laws Worldwide Now Cover More Than 70 Countries appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.titleOriginal: This Tourette’s wrist device cut tics by a quarter in a UK trial
items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Σε μια κλινική δοκιμή του 2023 σε 121 άτομα στο Ηνωμένο Βασίλειο, η χρήση μιας πρωτότυπης συσκευής καρπού μείωσε τη συχνότητα τικ κατά μέσο όρο 25 τοις εκατό. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM In a 2023 clinical trial of 121 people in the UK, wearing a prototype wrist device reduced tic frequency by an average of 25 percent. The Tourette’s wrist device, called Neupulse , came out of research at the University of Nottingham, and three years on, the people using it describe its effect in far stronger terms than a one-in-four reduction would suggest. How a Tourette’s wrist device targets tics Rhythmic pulses to the median nerve Neupulse sends rhythmic electrical pulses into the median nerve, which runs through the wrist and into the hand. Trials have shown that this stimulation changes activity in the brain regions responsible for movement control, and that the rhythm of the pulses can lower both the frequency and the intensity of tics. The device was developed by the university and its spin-out company, Neurotherapeutics Ltd, which secured £1 million (about $1.3 million) in additional funding to bring it to market. Stephen Jackson, the Nottingham professor who has led the research, described the response from users as “a dream come true.” Some of the feedback he has received is very concrete. “We’ve had people saying they managed to get through their wedding vows without ticking,” he said. Others told the team they could move through an airport and board a flight without tics. Tourette’s syndrome in the UK Tourette’s syndrome is a neurodevelopmental condition, usually beginning in childhood, that causes involuntary sounds and movements known as tics. More than 300,000 people in the UK have it, according to the charity Tourettes Action , and there is no cure. The condition reached a wider audience in 2023 when singer Lewis Capaldi, who has Tourette’s, tried the device before a concert in Nottingham, and again through the film I Swear , a drama based on the life of Tourette’s campaigner John Davidson. Three users, three measurable changes Katie, 15: years of constant vocal tics Katie, from Hertfordshire, started having tics at age seven. Her snorting tic ran almost nonstop, to the point of leaving her with a sore throat that kept her in bed for two weeks, and it disrupted her sleep, her eating, and her school attendance. “It was constantly moving, constantly making sounds and then I was kind of getting looked at like, ‘why are you doing that?'” she said. Her mom, Julia, called it “heartbreaking” to watch. “You feel helpless. You feel you don’t know where to turn really,” she said. After reading about the Nottingham research, Julia brought Katie to try the device in December, before it went on sale. The effect was immediate, Katie said, and she became “really calm.” “It was absolutely life-changing. It was like the best day of my life,” she said. On the drive back to Hertfordshire, she “just cried the whole way home.” Ollie, 15: a different diagnosis, a similar response Ollie’s case extends the picture, because he does not have Tourette’s. Nearly two years ago he cracked his neck, and about 48 hours later the movement had become involuntary and constant. “It was incredibly sudden,” he said. He was later diagnosed with functional neurological disorder (FND), a condition that affects how the brain sends and receives signals. His father, Alex, said sleeping, eating and drinking all became “incredibly difficult.” Ollie stayed inside for about a month at one stage and missed six to seven months of school ahead of his GCSEs, the exams British students sit around age 16. He came close to telling his parents not to bother with the device. A few months ago, when he switched it on for the first time, he phoned home. “You could hear that he was crying on the telephone because it had worked and his neck movement had stopped,” Alex said. Ollie put it this way: “It’s like a light switch. I remember my hands were quite shaky when I was calling my parents because it’s like getting part of your life back.” Mylo, 17: from trial participant to owner Mylo, from Buckinghamshire, was 13 when he joined the 2023 trial. He recently received his own device as a gift and said the urge to suppress his facial tics went away “instantaneously.” “As soon as it comes on, I can feel it,” he said. “I feel different… I feel new almost, which is strange.” Why Neupulse is not yet an NHS treatment Wellness product versus medical device The device comes in two versions. Neupulse-C is sold as a consumer wellness product, and the university says “thousands” have been purchased. Neupulse-M is the version intended for marketing as a medical treatment for tics and Tourette’s syndrome, and it is still working through regulatory approval. That distinction determines whether the National Health Service can offer it. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) has identified the technology as “promising” but asked for more evidence of long-term benefit. In 2025, it said its committee would meet again to assess the device’s clinical and cost-effectiveness. “They were unable to recommend it for use in the NHS until we have the regulatory approval,” Jackson said. “That’s something we’re working towards.” He hopes to see the Tourette’s wrist device available through the NHS “in the next year or so.” Early reports from the Tourette’s community Emma McNally, CEO of Tourettes Action , said the users she has spoken with have given the device “nothing but praise.” “Some people have said it’s helped them to go to places that they’ve not been for a long time, such as the cinema or a library,” she said. Others told her it helped them come out of a tic attack and feel more relaxed. Wrist stimulation beyond Tourette’s syndrome The Nottingham team is now testing the same approach on other conditions. Early trials have examined whether the pulses can reduce tremors in people with Parkinson’s , and Jackson said the university plans a UK-wide clinical trial covering anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). The next milestone is regulatory, since medical approval for Neupulse-M would open the door to NICE guidance and NHS prescriptions, and the trials that follow will show whether a signal sent through the wrist can shape movement and mood in conditions well beyond tics. items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM You know that feeling when it’s two in the afternoon, and you can’t quite account for where the morning went? Not because you weren’t doing things, but because the busyness didn’t add up to anything you can point to. It’s demoralizing in a specific way, and it has surprisingly little to do with how early your alarm went off. Time management experts Melinda Rathkopf, M.D., M.B.A. , and Julie Morgenstern , the author of multiple bestselling books on productivity, say most of what shapes your morning was set in motion the night before, and the solution is usually far simpler than the elaborate routines you’ve seen floating around online. Start the night before Where do both experts begin? The evening before. When you make decisions about tomorrow before you go to sleep, you take some of the friction out of the morning itself. “Preplanning the day ahead and making decisions ahead of time makes the rest of your day potentially calmer and less stressful,” says Rathkopf. “Set yourself up by knowing what’s coming.” Transition time is one of the things that tends to get left out when people plan their days. It’s easy to schedule back-to-back tasks and forget that moving between them really does take time. Build that in the night before and the morning feels a lot less like you’re already behind before you’ve started. This extends to sleep, too. Rathkopf recommends starting with how much sleep you genuinely need to feel refreshed, then working backward from your wake time to set a consistent bedtime. “ Sleep is so vital to daily functioning and brain health,” she says. Most people schedule everything else first and try to fit sleep in around it. She suggests reversing that. Put the phone away before bed and after waking up If there’s one habit both experts come back to, it’s keeping your phone out of your first and last hour of each day. Morgenstern is direct about it. “The number one thing that can boost morning productivity has to do with screen time ,” she says. “We should not be on our devices an hour before bed, and we should not be on our devices for our first hour of the morning.” Checking your phone first thing does more than eat up time. It pulls you into a reactive state before you’ve had a chance to figure out your own priorities for the day. “The phone can be a useful tool, but it’s designed to keep us on there,” Morgenstern says. “Think of it like sugar — you have to really manage your consumption, and take charge. It’s the key to morning productivity, engagement, your relationships, everything.” She recommends replacing that screen time with something restorative: reading, getting outside, or having a conversation with someone. The goal isn’t deprivation; it’s starting the day on your own terms instead of somebody else’s notifications. Keep your routine simple One persistent myth about productive mornings is that they require an elaborate ritual. If you’ve ever felt vaguely inadequate watching someone describe their two-hour routine involving cold plunges , journaling, and a complicated smoothie, you’re not alone. Those routines often backfire. “It can make you stressed out — ‘Oh god, I didn’t meditate long enough!'” Morgenstern says. “Add three to four elements maximum for a morning routine. Otherwise, you’re habituating to something that’s unsustainable.” Find the small handful of things that reliably start your morning feeling calm and grounded, and stick with those. If you’re getting ready alongside young children, Morgenstern suggests completing your own routine before they’re up, then putting some thought into making their mornings smoother too. Laying out clothes or choosing breakfast the night before can take a surprising amount of stress out of a weekday morning. Train your brain with predictability Your brain is a creature of habit in the most useful sense. “Our brains love predictability,” says Rathkopf. “When you have a predictable routine, you’re reducing your stress and cognitive load.” When your morning follows a consistent pattern, you spend less mental energy on logistics and more on the work itself, which sounds obvious until you notice how rarely most mornings feel that way in practice. Morgenstern describes building a regular block for deep thinking as a kind of training for your brain: “If you have a predictable head-down time, your brain gets acclimated to it — it’s 10:30, that’s when we do our deep thinking. I’ve never seen anyone build proactive work with an erratic schedule.” For creative work especially, consistency turns out to matter more than inspiration. Start with the work that matters most A lot of mornings get swallowed by emails, messages, and reactive tasks before you ever reach work that needs your purest attention. “The number one difficulty people have is that the day starts off all reactive, and they can’t get to proactive work,” Morgenstern says. Her suggestion is to start with the most important thing on your list, the one that needs your freshest thinking. Even if everything else gets away from you after that, you’ve done something that mattered. “Even if you only get that one thing done, you’ll feel the greatest sense of relief that you’ve done your job,” she says. If your workplace opens with a morning meeting, Morgenstern recommends blocking off a half hour to an hour right after it for focused work, to address anything that came out of the meeting before settling into your main task. Better yet, see if you can get your whole team to protect the first hour of the day. Build in small moments of recovery Self-care doesn’t need to be a whole thing. What Morgenstern recommends is more modest: short pauses woven throughout the day, especially during your busiest stretches. “Add microbursts of self-care in your day — five to 20-minute activities that recharge you,” she says. A short walk, some music on your commute, ten minutes with a book. Small enough to fit into almost any day, and consistent enough to keep you from burning out by three in the afternoon. “The harder you’re working, the harder you have to recover,” she says. Stopping feels like the last thing you can afford when you’re slammed, but that’s usually when it matters most. Give yourself room to change, and to have off days Both experts caution against treating your morning routine as something fixed. Life changes, seasons change, your circumstances shift, and what works at one stage may not work at another. “You may need to change it based on other obligations, at different stages of your life, or even in different seasons,” says Rathkopf. And when a morning doesn’t come together the way you hoped, she has one more piece of advice: don’t be hard on yourself about it. “Everybody’s different, and what you’re seeing in posts is someone else’s best versions and best days,” Rathkopf says. “They have those not-so-perfect days, too.” A morning routine isn’t something you get right once. It’s something you keep adjusting until it fits. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Recommendations are independently selected by our team but may result in a commission to Nice News which helps keep our content free. We likely all have a person in our lives who’s impossibly hard to shop for. Maybe they’re the family member who says they “don’t want anything” or the friend who seems to already have it all. You can go two routes for recipients like these: Get them something practical (items that make life a little easier) or not so practical (gifts intended simply to delight). To help with your search this holiday season, we rounded up a mix of both. And if you’re still on the hunt for the right present after perusing this guide, check out the Nice News team’s favorite products of the year for more ideas. Aura Digital Picture Frame For the sentimentalist who always asks for more photos Courtesy of Aura A sweet gift for loved ones near and far, Aura’s digital frames let people share photos from multiple phones and then display them like a slideshow. My sister and I each have one, and it’s a thrill to see new pics of my niece and nephew pop up on mine. For those who prefer tangible photos, consider pairing a fun frame with this compact printer that makes 4-by-6-inch prints directly from a smartphone. Shop Aura Shop Amazon Soligt Wooden Cookbook and Tablet Stand For the one who uses their iPad to pull up recipes in the kitchen Courtesy of Amazon This nifty stand is ideal for holding medium-sized cookbooks as well as iPads, Kindles, and other tablets. It features a kickstand you can position at multiple angles, and its elegant cutting board-esque design helps it blend in with other kitchen accoutrements. Your recipient can use it to watch tutorials or read recipes — or to FaceTime you while they’re cooking. Shop AMAZON La Lune Upcycled Leather Crossbody Bag For the stylish friend who’s always on the go Courtesy of La Lune Everyone needs a purse — and this one from La Lune couldn’t be more practical. The vivid Electric Blue Crossbody fits a phone, wallet, keys, sunglasses, and lip balm, making it an easy pick for errands, sightseeing, or a dinner out. Handcrafted by Los Angeles artisans from upcycled Italian leather, each vintage-inspired bag from La Lune comes from a limited supply of leftover leather with its own color and grain that softens with wear. It’s a gift as distinctive as the person who will carry it, and it will last for years to come.* Shop La Lune *Indicates a Nice News brand partnership or affiliate Bee Cups Watering Stations For the gardener who wants to attract more wildlife to their yard Courtesy of Bee Cups Bee Cups are patented watering stations, and they happen to be both practical and whimsical. Each cup holds about a teaspoon of water — just enough to hydrate a visiting bee or butterfly while preventing them from getting submerged. They’re handmade from 100% porcelain, so they’ll hold up in changing weather conditions, and painted with a special UV-reactive glaze to mimic flowers, so they’re extra enticing to pollinators. Shop Bee Cups SHOP AMAZON Fitbit Air For the person who wants to track their steps without getting distracted by notifications Courtesy of Google Think of this as a yoga-class-friendly fitness tracker. It delivers the benefits of typical trackers — like monitoring steps, sleep, and heart rate — but it’s screen-free, with no buttons or notifications (the data is accessible via a companion app). It’s also water-resistant, and a single five-minute charge can last up to a week. Tip: Include a few replacement straps with the gift so your recipient can select the best color for their outfit on any given day. Shop GOogle SHOP AMAZON Ban.do Quilted Blanket For the one who loves a cozy night in Courtesy of Ban.do This quilt is as cozy as it is cheerful. It’s soft, machine washable, and a sweet way to help someone stay snug. Check out the brand’s other four designs, which are equally as delightful to look at. Shop Ban.do Terrain Forget-Me-Not Flower Press For the crafty soul Courtesy of Terrain Hobby gifts can be hit-or-miss, but this one’s sure to go over well with gardeners and flower lovers. It comes with everything needed to start preserving blooms (sans the blooms themselves) in one very pretty package. They can then use the pressed flowers to make things like coasters, jewelry, and boho decor . If you think your loved one would rather skip over the DIY component, consider this lovely preserved flowers keepsake box or picture frame . Shop Terrain Loop Earplugs For the concertgoer who’s concerned about their hearing Courtesy of Loop Know someone with misophonia — or a pal who simply wants to protect their hearing? Loop earplugs lower the decibel level of noise (to varying degrees based on the different models), and work wonders for focusing, calming an overstimulated nervous system, enjoying concerts without damaging your eardrums, and sleeping. Each pair comes with a handy case and four sets of washable, silicone ear tips. Shop Loop Shop AMAZon Cabin Nine 20-Minute Candles For the analog enthusiast Courtesy of Cabin Nine Who knew a timer could be so lovely? This set includes 12 small beeswax candles that each burn for approximately 20 minutes, as well as a reusable candle holder, matches, and a charming blue tin to keep everything in. It’s ideal for anyone who wants to carve out more time for journaling, reading, meditating, or yoga without relying on a digital timer. Shop Cabin nine Algae Cooking Club Nara’s Roasted Garlic Oil For the home chef who doesn’t like the smell of garlic on their fingers Courtesy of Algae Cooking Club For the foodies, this oil gives dishes all the flavor of garlic without them having to actually chop any garlic. It’s made primarily from algae, which has an extremely high smoke-point (higher than avocado oil) and is infused with garlic, yuzu, miso, and scallions. In other words, it’s delicious and can be used for sautéing, roasting, drizzling, you name it. Shop algae cooking club Shop AMAZON Audible Membership For the bookworm who loves to listen to their literature Courtesy of Audible Got a friend with a never-ending TBR list? An Audible gift membership lets them download an audiobook each month from a catalog of over 1 million titles. If they already have a login, that’s no problem — they’ll just receive more credits to use. You can give three months for $45, six months for $90, or a full year of reading for $150 (with no automatic auto-renew). It comes quite in handy when they’re 135th in line for a library book in the Libby app. Optional: Pair the membership with this silly mug . shop Audible SHOP AMAZON America the Beautiful Parks Pass For the nature lover Courtesy of Recreation.Gov Another blend of practical and delightful, the America the Beautiful Pass covers entrance fees and standard amenity fees (aka day-use fees) at more than 2,000 national parks and federal recreational sites for one year. The digital version is convenient, but you can add in a physical card at checkout for people who might prefer to keep the pass in their car’s glove compartment. Shop Recreation.gov Baggu Packing Cubes For the frequent traveler Courtesy of Baggu A packing cube goes a long way, particularly for overpackers who could use a little help squeezing just one more thing into their bag. Baggu’s cubes are a favorite of Staff Editor Ally Mauch, who says “you’d be amazed at how much you can fit in these.” The cherry on top? They come in such fun, punchy patterns and colors. Shop Baggu Shop Amazon Board For the avid game night host Courtesy of Board Where to start with this snazzy gift? It’s a “face-to-face game console” that’s designed to be a happy medium between digital games and board games. The touchscreen device lays flat on a table and comes with physical pieces that interact with the screen, so players can gather around for a classic yet modern game night experience. It includes a built-in starter pack of seven games, and tons more can be purchased with no subscription required. Oh, and it made Time magazine’s Best Inventions of 2026 list. Shop Board Q uokka Hotel Wildeluxe 1,000-Piece Puzzle For the one who loves a good challenge Courtesy of Amazon This is no ordinary puzzle. It doubles as a mystery game with 321 “secrets” that are unlocked by putting together the 1,000 pieces, opening the riddle envelopes, and listening to an accompanying audio story. It’s gotten rave reviews, and it’s under $25. Shop AMAZON Related: 19 Gifts for Readers Who Always Have Their Nose in a Book

Ο προβληματισμός της δεν φτάνει ως συμβουλή αλλά ως άδεια: να νιώθει ημιτελής και ολοκληρωμένη ταυτόχρονα, να σταματήσει να περιμένει…
items.descriptionOriginal: At twenty-two, Haile Thomas sat with a question most of us quietly carry for decades: what do I do with all of this existence? Rather than answer it, she did something braver -- she wrote her way into the uncertainty itself. Her reflection arrives not as advice but as permission: to feel incomplete and whole at the same time, to stop waiting for the map that will never come. She offers a quietly radical image of identity -- that growing up is less about finding yourself than noticing "the entity that gets dressed," the spaciousness beneath every costume we try on and discard. There is no finish line in her telling, only transformations meeting us in the moments we least expect. "Growing up is a never ending journey," she writes -- and somehow that lands not as defeat but as relief. What she offers, finally, is not wisdom so much as weather: a loosening, a liquefying of the hard certainties we grip when life refuses to hold still.

items.descriptionOriginal: A stick figure family, a googly-eyed monster, a happy rainbow. Children’s artwork represents how they see the world at any given age — a sweet, fleeting perspective that the adults in their lives yearn to preserve. But kids are prolific creators, so what’s to be done with all these construction paper canvases as more continuously flood in? Artist Shana Blakley came up with a creative way to save her kids’ drawings while breaking out of a rut she’d been in with her own work: She turned them into a big, colorful collage to hang in her family’s home. When she shared the result on Instagram, her comment section exploded. The idea clearly resonated with other moms, dads, and grandparents. Heirloom Collage Shana Blakley’s first kids’ artwork collage “We want to honor what our kids make,” Blakley told Nice News, adding: “Nearly every parent around the world has a growing pile of kid art, and it’s in our nature to save it. We feel guilty throwing it away, but storing it also begins to feel unsettling. There comes a time when you realize how much of it you have and you ask yourself: ‘What am I keeping this for?’” Heirloom Collage Molly Revers with her grandkids and the collages made from their artwork Shortly after posting the piece last year, she launched Heirloom Collage and started taking commissions. Now, she offers an online course that guides participants in producing their own artist-quality collages out of kiddos’ creations. The course consists of six video modules totaling one hour, and Blakley provides feedback in a private Facebook group where students can post their in-progress and completed work. Molly Revers enjoys dabbling in different artistic endeavors, so she signed up for the $99 e-course. “The most meaningful aspect was the joy it brought me when creating the collages and the joy it brought my little grandsons when they saw their work displayed in such a cool way,” she shared. “They love picking their favorite creations and memories associated with them.” Heirloom Collage Another parent’s completed collage For Blakley, who lives in Richmond, Virginia, and began her career as a fine artist over a decade ago, the project reconnected her to a sense of spontaneity after a period of creative stagnation. “Halfway through it, I recall thinking, ‘[My kids] didn’t second-guess their creativity in these pieces, so I shouldn’t either,’” she said. “That was a big breakthrough for me.” It’s something many adults, artists or not, can relate to. “A lot of my students haven’t made art since they were kids, and this brings them back to it,” Blakley added. Overall, though, the memorable shared experience of making that first collage with her two children — the youngsters helped select the included drawings and “were buzzing with pride” — is what she wishes for her clients. “That connection is what lasts, and they end up with something their family really treasures,” she said. Heirloom Collage Jeanine Long-Tuohy with her granddaughter Ava and the collage they made Jeanine Long-Tuohy, who loves her granddaughter Ava’s artwork, created her first piece with Ava’s help and has since started a new one with another grandchild. “Working on this made me feel like there’s a lot more we can do together,” Long-Tuohy said. “It’s a memory they will always have of me.”

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.description: Η νόσος Lafora είναι μια σπάνια γενετική πάθηση που συνήθως επηρεάζει παιδιά και εφήβους, προκαλώντας συχνές κρίσεις και σταδιακή απώλεια της γνωστικής λειτουργίας. Δεν υπάρχει θεραπεία, επομένως η εστίαση για πολλούς γονείς αναπόφευκτα στρέφεται στην ποιότητα ζωής. Αυτό είναι κάτι που η μαμά του Ντιτρόιτ η Azeza Kasham πάλευε να διατηρήσει για τον 17χρονο γιο της, Gigi Breadiy.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .
